back:
Atrophy and pendulousness.
* Loss of estrogenic stimulation causes regression of the ductile system.
* Loss of progestational stimulation causes regression of the lobule-alveolar system.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Contrast the pattern of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) pulses in childhood versus the postmenopausal state.
back:
* **Childhood:** Hypothalamus does not secrete significant quantities of GnRH.
* **Postmenopause:** GnRH pulses continue, but pituitary FSH and LH are produced in large, non-cyclical quantities due to lack of ovarian feedback.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: State the effect of postmenopausal estrogen deficiency on total body metabolism and fat distribution.
back:
* **Metabolism:** Slight decrease in whole-body metabolic rate.
* **Fat Distribution:** Increased fat deposition, particularly in subcutaneous tissues.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: The fundamental cause of menopause is the depletion of [primordial follicles], leading to the eventual cessation of ovarian estrogen and progesterone production.
back:
• Ovaries "burn out" as remaining follicles reach zero.
• Estrogen production falls below critical inhibitory levels.
• Gonadotropin-releasing hormone inhibition is lost.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: A 55-year-old female presents with a bone density scan showing significant demineralization. This skeletal deterioration is driven by a menopausal increase in [osteoclastic] activity.
back:
• Estrogen deficiency increases osteoclast number and lifespan.
• Loss of estrogen reduces osteoprotegerin (OPG) production.
• Results in decreased bone matrix and increased fracture risk.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Explain the physiological mechanism responsible for the massive elevation of FSH and LH levels following menopause.
back:
• Depletion of follicles leads to a fall in estrogen/progesterone.
• Loss of negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary.
• FSH and LH (especially FSH) are produced in continuous, large quantities.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Contrast the histological appearance of the vaginal epithelium in a reproductive-age female with that of a postmenopausal female.
back:
• Reproductive: Thick, stratified squamous epithelium resistant to trauma/infection.
• Postmenopausal: Thin, atrophic epithelium (often cuboidal-like) that is easily damaged.
• Leads to increased risk of vaginal infections and irritation.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: List the primary morphological changes occurring in the uterus and fallopian tubes during the menopausal transition.
back:
• Uterus: Regresses to a smaller, infantile-like size.
• Fallopian Tubes: Mucosal lining becomes thin and secretory activity ceases.
• Myometrium: Undergoes atrophy due to withdrawal of estrogenic stimulation.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: The common menopausal symptom known as the "hot flush" is characterized by [extreme flushing of the skin] and results from vasomotor instability.
back:
• Caused by withdrawal of estrogen effect on thermoregulatory centers.
• Characterized by sudden skin flushing and perspiration.
• Often accompanied by psychic sensations of dyspnea.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: A 60-year-old female has non-functional ovaries but still possesses a baseline level of circulating estrone. Identify the primary source of this postmenopausal estrogen.
back:
• Derived from androgens secreted by the adrenal cortices.
• Peripheral conversion occurs in the liver and adipose tissue.
• Androstenedione is aromatized into estrone in non-ovarian tissues.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Describe the physiological regression of the female breasts following the withdrawal of ovarian steroids in menopause.
back:
• Estrogen loss leads to atrophy of the mammary ductal system.
• Progesterone withdrawal causes regression of breast lobules and alveoli.
• Glandular tissue is replaced by connective tissue, making breasts pendulous.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Contrast the pattern of urinary gonadotropin excretion in childhood versus the postmenopausal state.
back:
• Childhood: Extremely low levels due to hypothalamic inactivity.
• Postmenopause: Very high, continuous levels due to loss of follicular feedback.
• Reflects a fundamental shift from steroid-inhibited to uninhibited pituitary function.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Identify the psychological and systemic triad of symptoms frequently associated with the physiological decline of estrogen during menopause.
back:
• Irritability and anxiety.
• Fatigue and extreme somnolence.
• Psychic sensations of dyspnea (shortness of breath).

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: The cessation of the female sexual cycle during menopause is primarily caused by the "burning out" of the [___], where production of [___] falls virtually to zero.
back:
• Ovaries
• Estrogens
• This occurs as the number of primordial follicles approaches zero, typically between age 40 and 50.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: A 52-year-old female reports sudden intense skin flushing and an overwhelming sense of warmth. These vasomotor symptoms are a direct physiological consequence of [___] withdrawal.
back:
• Estrogen
• These "hot flushes" occur in approximately 15% of women.
• They represent a failure of vasomotor stability during hormonal readjustment.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Explain the physiological basis for the development of "psychic dyspnea" and irritability during the menopausal transition.
back:
• Loss of estrogenic and progestogenic stimulation.
• The body must readjust from a life of cyclic hormonal pulses to a state devoid of them.
• Results in fatigue, anxiety, and sensations of breathlessness.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Contrast the skeletal dynamics of a postmenopausal woman with her premenopausal state regarding osteoclastic activity and bone matrix.
back:
• Postmenopause: Increased osteoclastic activity due to estrogen deficiency.
• Pre-menopause: Estrogen inhibits osteoclasts and stimulates bone growth.
• Result: Decreased bone matrix and deposition of calcium/phosphate.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Describe the trophic changes that occur in the uterus and breast tissues following the onset of menopause.
back:
• Uterus: Involution occurs, regressing to an almost infantile size.
• Breasts: Atrophy and become pendulous due to regression of the ductal system.
• Stroma: Significant loss of fat and stromal mass.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: During menopause, the vaginal epithelium changes from a robust stratified type back to a thin, fragile layer, making the woman highly susceptible to [___].
back:
• Vaginal infections
• Local trauma
• The loss of estrogen reduces the protective thickness and secretory capacity of the epithelium.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: A 55-year-old woman presents with high levels of circulating FSH and LH. Relate these lab findings to the specific failure of the ovarian feedback loop in menopause.
back:
• Atretic follicles fail to produce estrogen.
• Lack of estrogen removes the negative feedback on the anterior pituitary.
• FSH and LH are produced in large, continuous quantities.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Detail the mechanism by which estrogen deficiency in menopause leads to an increased risk of bone fractures.
back:
• Estrogen normally stimulates osteoprotegerin (inhibits bone resorption).
• Deficiency increases osteoclast number/activity.
• Leads to osteoporosis, especially affecting vertebrae and long bone strength.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Contrast the changes in skin texture and vascularity between a premenopausal woman and a postmenopausal woman.
back:
• Premenopause: Skin is soft, smooth, and highly vascular (warm).
• Postmenopause: Skin texture thickens compared to childhood but loses the protective estrogenic texture/vascularity.
• Often associated with increased wrinkling.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: Identify the primary source of the small amounts of estrogens still present in a postmenopausal woman's urine.
back:
• Peripheral conversion of androgens.
• Adrenal cortices secrete minute amounts of androgens converted in tissues.
• Ovarian production itself falls to virtually zero.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: The fundamental physiological cause of menopause is the 'burning out' of the ovaries, which is characterized by the depletion of [___].
back: - Primordial follicles. - Throughout life, only ~400 follicles mature while hundreds of thousands undergo atresia, eventually exhausting the functional pool.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: A 52-year-old female presents with frequent hot flushes and amenorrhea. Lab tests show markedly elevated serum FSH. Identify the primary pathophysiology.
back: - Exhaustion of functional ovarian follicles. - Loss of estrogen-mediated negative feedback on the pituitary. - Resultant hypersecretion of gonadotropic hormones.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
coreConcept: Loss of Negative Feedback in Menopause
front: Explain why gonadotropin levels (FSH and LH) rise sharply and remain high during the postmenopausal period.
back: - Ovarian estrogen production falls virtually to zero. - This removes the negative feedback inhibition on the anterior pituitary. - Gonadotropes produce massive, continuous quantities of FSH and LH.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: Contrast the physiological status of the anterior pituitary in a prepubertal child versus a postmenopausal woman regarding FSH secretion.
back: - Prepubertal: FSH is extremely low due to high hypothalamic sensitivity to trace steroids. - Postmenopausal: FSH is extremely high due to follicular exhaustion and feedback loss.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: Identify the primary reason the monthly sexual cycle becomes irregular and then ceases during the transition to menopause.
back: - Primordial follicle count falls below a critical threshold. - Estrogen production becomes inconsistent and insufficient to trigger the LH surge. - Cycles become anovulatory before stopping entirely.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: In the postmenopausal state, the specific gonadotropin that shows the most significant and abrupt increase in urinary excretion is [___].
back: - Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH). - LH also increases, but FSH is the primary diagnostic marker for identifying ovarian failure.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: A 49-year-old woman is treated for infertility with high-dose gonadotropins, but her estradiol levels remain low and follicles fail to grow. Explain this failure.
back: - Ovarian 'burn out' or follicle exhaustion. - The absence of functional primordial follicles means there are no target cells to respond to FSH/LH stimulus.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: Explain the cellular mechanism of follicular atresia as it relates to the onset of menopause.
back: - Follicles degenerate continually from birth regardless of cycle activity. - By age 45, the follicular pool is nearly approaching zero. - Depletion terminates the capacity for steroidogenesis and ovulation.

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: Contrast the hormonal profile of a normal luteal phase with the postmenopausal state regarding steroid levels.
back: - Luteal phase: High progesterone and moderate estrogen (feedback active). - Menopause: Virtually zero progesterone and estrogen (feedback absent).

category: Explain the cause of menopause
front: Define the primary physiological event that signifies the 'burning out' of the ovaries.
back: - Approaching zero functional primordial follicles. - Loss of ovarian estrogen and progesterone production. - Disruption of the rhythmic hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: The placental transport of glucose into fetal blood occurs via [___], resulting in fetal glucose levels that remain 20% to 30% lower than maternal concentrations.
back:
● Facilitated diffusion
● Mediated by carrier molecules in the trophoblast cells
● Driven by the concentration gradient between mother and fetus

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: A fetus maintains adequate oxygenation despite a maternal sinus P_{O2} of only 50 mmHg. The primary mechanism allowing fetal blood to carry 20-50% more oxygen than maternal blood at this pressure is the specific presence of [___].
back:
● Fetal hemoglobin (HbF)
● HbF has a higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin
● It causes a leftward shift in the oxygen dissociation curve

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Explain the role of the "Double Bohr Effect" in facilitating placental gas exchange.
back:
● CO2 loss makes fetal blood alkaline, increasing its O2 affinity
● CO2 gain makes maternal blood acidic, decreasing its O2 affinity
● These simultaneous shifts favor O2 transfer to the fetus

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Contrast the placental transport mechanisms used for glucose versus those used for fatty acids.
back:
● Glucose: Facilitated diffusion via carriers in trophoblasts
● Fatty Acids: Simple diffusion due to high lipid solubility in membranes
● Fatty acids diffuse more slowly than glucose despite solubility

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Identify the three primary non-protein nitrogenous waste products excreted from the fetus into the maternal blood via the placenta.
back:
● Urea (diffuses with great ease)
● Uric acid
● Creatinine (diffuses less easily; requires higher fetal concentration)

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: In the mature placenta, fetal blood circulates through capillaries within [___], which are bathed in maternal blood from the uterine arteries in the intervillous spaces.
back:
● Placental villi
● Trophoblast projections extending into maternal sinuses
● Forms the primary site for nutrient and gas exchange

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: A neonate is found to have a significantly higher blood concentration of creatinine compared to the mother. Explain why this gradient is necessary for placental excretion.
back:
● Creatinine does not diffuse across the placenta easily
● Excretion depends on a high fetal-to-maternal concentration gradient
● Contrast: Urea diffuses easily with only a slight gradient

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Explain the two primary physical changes that cause placental diffusion conductance to increase toward the end of pregnancy.
back:
● Expansion of the total surface area of the placental villi
● Thinning of the membrane diffusion layers in the villi
● Result: Massive increase in total diffusing capacity

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Contrast the P_{O2} and P_{CO2} gradients that drive gas exchange across the placental membrane at term.
back:
● O2: Gradient of ~20 mmHg (Maternal sinus 50 mmHg to Fetal blood 30 mmHg)
● CO2: Gradient of ~2-3 mmHg (Fetal blood higher than maternal sinus)
● CO2 diffuses 20x faster than O2 due to extreme solubility

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Why is the total hemoglobin concentration of fetal blood significant for its non-hormonal respiratory function?
back:
● Fetal hemoglobin concentration is ~50% higher than the mother's
● Enhances the total amount of oxygen transported to fetal tissues
● Complements the Bohr effect and HbF affinity properties

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: The physiological decline in [___] secretion during menopause leads to increased osteoclastic activity and a subsequent decrease in bone matrix and calcification.
back:
• Estrogen (specifically ̢-estradiol).
• Estrogen normally stimulates osteoprotegerin to inhibit bone resorption.
• Its deficiency creates an imbalance where resorption exceeds deposition, resulting in postmenopausal osteoporosis.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: A 52-year-old female reports sudden sensations of extreme warmth, skin flushing, and psychic dyspnea. Identify the clinical phenomenon and the physiological trigger behind these vasomotor symptoms.
back:
• Hot flushes.
• Caused by instability in the hypothalamic thermoregulatory centers.
• Triggered by the abrupt withdrawal of estrogen and the associated surge in pituitary gonadotropins.

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
coreConcept: FSH Diagnostic Utility in Ovarian Failure
front: Explain the physiological basis for using the measurement of serum FSH to diagnose menopause versus anovulatory cycles in younger reproductive-age women.
back:
• Menopause: FSH is chronically elevated due to total loss of ovarian follicles and negative feedback inhibition.
• Anovulation: FSH is often low or normal as follicles are still present.
• Menopause reflects primary ovarian failure ('burning out').

category: Discuss the physiological changes in the function of the body at the time of menopause
front: A 48-year-old female with irregular menses is contrasted with a 55-year-old postmenopausal female. Distinguish the physiological state of their ovarian follicles and their expected steroidogenic response to exogenous FSH administration.
back:
• 48-year-old: Few responsive follicles remain; exogenous FSH can still stimulate estrogen production.
• 55-year-old: Follicles are atretic ('burnt out').
• Response: The postmenopausal ovary is refractory to FSH; estrogen levels remain low despite maximal stimulation.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: In the placental membrane, glucose is transported from maternal blood to fetal blood via the process of [___].
back:
• Facilitated diffusion
• Mediated by carrier molecules in trophoblast cells
• Necessary because fetal glucose levels are 20-30% lower than maternal concentrations.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: A neonate is born with an umbilical vein P O2 of 30 mmHg. Despite this low partial pressure, the fetus avoided hypoxia in utero primarily due to the high concentration of [___] and the [___] effect.
back:
• Fetal Hemoglobin (HbF)
• Double Bohr Effect
• HbF carries 20-50% more oxygen than maternal Hb at low partial pressures.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Explain how the 'Double Bohr Effect' carries out its biological function during placental gas exchange.
back:
• Fetal CO2 loss makes fetal blood alkaline, increasing O2 affinity
• Maternal CO2 gain makes maternal blood acidic, decreasing O2 affinity
• This maximizes O2 loading in the fetus and unloading from the mother.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Contrast the placental excretion of urea with that of creatinine from the fetus to the maternal circulation.
back:
• Urea: Diffuses with great ease; fetal levels only slightly exceed maternal levels
• Creatinine: Diffuses less easily; fetal concentrations are significantly higher than maternal
• Both move via simple diffusion gradients.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Describe the transition from trophoblastic nutrition to placental diffusion during the early stages of pregnancy.
back:
• Trophoblastic period: Digestion of decidual cells (dominant for 8 weeks)
• Placental diffusion: Starts by day 16 post-fertilization
• Diffusion becomes primary as placental surface area and permeability increase.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: The mean P O2 of maternal blood in placental sinuses is approximately [___] mmHg, providing a pressure gradient of [___] mmHg for oxygen diffusion into fetal blood.
back:
• 50 mmHg (Maternal)
• 20 mmHg (Gradient)
• This gradient drives oxygen into fetal capillaries where P O2 is roughly 30 mmHg.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: An Rh-negative mother is carrying an Rh-positive fetus. Identify the non-hormonal placental event that allows fetal erythrocytes to enter maternal circulation, potentially causing erythroblastosis fetalis.
back:
• Breaks in the placental membrane
• Occurs rarely during pregnancy but more common during delivery
• Allows passage of fetal cells into maternal sinuses across the trophoblastic barrier.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Specify the three primary factors that allow fetal blood to transport adequate oxygen despite a low P O2 leaving the placenta.
back:
• High HbF oxygen affinity (left-shifted curve)
• High fetal hemoglobin concentration (50% greater than maternal)
• Double Bohr Effect optimizing placental gas exchange.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Contrast the transport mechanics of glucose versus fatty acids across the placental membrane.
back:
• Glucose: Facilitated diffusion via trophoblast carrier proteins
• Fatty acids: Simple diffusion due to high lipid solubility
• Fatty acids diffuse more slowly than glucose despite higher solubility.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Identify the primary non-protein nitrogenous waste products that diffuse from fetal blood into maternal blood through the placenta.
back:
• Urea
• Uric acid
• Creatinine
• These move according to concentration gradients as fetal levels are higher than maternal levels.

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: The primary metabolic substrate used to energize fetal growth is glucose, which is transported across the placental membrane via [___].
back:
• Facilitated diffusion
• Trophoblast cells use carrier molecules to transport glucose
• This allows adequate supply even though fetal glucose levels remain 20-30% lower than maternal levels

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: A neonate born to a mother with high titers of IgG antibodies against diphtheria shows temporary immunity to the disease for several months. This non-hormonal placental function is characterized by [___].
back:
• Passive immunity
• Selective transport of maternal protein antibodies (IgG) into the fetal blood
• This provides the infant protection against major childhood infectious diseases for the first six months of life

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Explain how the 'Double Bohr Effect' facilitates oxygen transfer from maternal sinuses to fetal blood.
back:
• Maternal blood loses O2 and gains fetal CO2, becoming more acidic and decreasing its O2 affinity
• Fetal blood loses CO2 to the mother, becoming more alkaline and increasing its O2 affinity
• These simultaneous shifts maximize the oxygen pressure gradient

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Contrast the placental clearance of urea with that of creatinine from the fetal circulation.
back:
• Urea: Diffuses with great ease; fetal concentrations are only slightly higher than maternal levels
• Creatinine: Diffuses less easily; fetal concentrations remain significantly higher than maternal levels
• Both rely on simple diffusion gradients across the placental membrane

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Identify two physical adaptations of the placental membrane during late pregnancy that dramatically increase its diffusion conductance.
back:
• Progressive thinning of the membrane diffusion layers
• Massive expansion of the total placental surface area
• These changes occur to meet the exponentially increasing respiratory and nutritional demands of the maturing fetus

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: The total diffusing capacity of the entire placenta for [___] at term is approximately 1.2 ml per minute per mm Hg partial pressure difference across the membrane.
back:
• Oxygen
• This capacity is comparable to the diffusing capacity of the newborn baby's own lungs
• It is driven by a mean pressure gradient of approximately 20 mm Hg

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: A pregnant patient develops sudden-onset hypertension and proteinuria. The underlying non-hormonal placental pathology involves failure of the trophoblasts to [___].
back:
• Adequately remodel maternal spiral arteries
• These vessels fail to transform into large, low-resistance, high-flow conduits
• Resultant placental ischemia triggers the release of anti-angiogenic factors into maternal circulation

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Describe the mechanism that allows carbon dioxide to be excreted efficiently across the placenta despite a very small PCO2 gradient of only 2-3 mm Hg.
back:
• Carbon dioxide is extremely soluble in the placental membrane
• It diffuses approximately 20 times as rapidly as oxygen
• This high solubility compensates for the narrow pressure gradient between fetal and maternal blood

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: Contrast the placental transport mechanisms of fatty acids with those of electrolytes (sodium and potassium).
back:
• Fatty acids: Highly lipid-soluble; diffuse directly through cell membranes, though more slowly than glucose
• Electrolytes: Water-soluble; diffuse with relative ease through the membrane pores
• Both depend primarily on their respective concentration gradients between mother and fetus

category: Explain the non-hormonal functions of placenta
front: List three physiological factors that enable fetal blood to transport adequate oxygen despite leaving the placenta at a PO2 of only 30 mm Hg.
back:
• High concentration of fetal hemoglobin (HbF), which is 50% greater than maternal levels
• HbF has a higher O2 affinity (left-shifted curve) than adult hemoglobin
• The Double Bohr Effect enhances oxygen uptake in the placental sinuses

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: The specific placental hormone responsible for preventing the involution of the corpus luteum immediately after implantation is [___].
back:
Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG).

- Secreted by syncytiotrophoblast cells.
- Maintains estrogen and progesterone secretion.
- Can be measured 8–9 days after ovulation.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: Corpus Luteum Necessity in Early Pregnancy
front: A pregnant woman at 8 weeks gestation undergoes a bilateral oophorectomy. Based on the source of steroid hormones at this stage, explain the likely effect on the pregnancy.
back:
Spontaneous abortion.

- The corpus luteum is essential for pregnancy until the 7th–12th week.
- Placental progesterone/estrogen production is insufficient to maintain the endometrium early on.
- Removal leads to sloughing of the decidua.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Explain the role of Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS) in maternal glucose metabolism.
back:
It acts as a metabolic "glucose sparer":

- Decreases maternal insulin sensitivity.
- Reduces maternal glucose utilization.
- Mobilizes free fatty acids from maternal stores.
- Ensures glucose remains available for fetal growth.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Contrast the synthetic pathway of estrogens in the ovaries with that of the placenta regarding precursor usage.
back:
Placenta vs Ovary:

- Ovary: Synthesizes estrogens de novo from cholesterol via aromatase.
- Placenta: Cannot synthesize estrogens de novo; it must convert DHEA precursors from fetal and maternal adrenal glands.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: State the primary physiological function of placental progesterone regarding uterine myometrial activity.
back:
Decreases uterine contractility:

- Reduces the frequency and intensity of contractions.
- Inhibits expulsion of the implanted fetus.
- Opposes the contractile effects of estrogen to maintain pregnancy.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: During gestation, the fetal adrenal cortex (fetal zone) primarily secretes [___], which is used by the placenta to produce estriol.
back:
Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA).

- Provided by fetal and maternal adrenal glands.
- Transported by blood to the placenta.
- Converted by syncytiotrophoblasts into estradiol, estrone, and estriol.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: A woman in her third trimester presents with significant generalized edema and increased blood volume. Which placental and adrenal hormones contribute to this physiological water retention?
back:
Estrogen and Aldosterone.

- Estrogen levels increase 30-fold, promoting salt and water retention.
- Aldosterone secretion doubles by term.
- Both increase renal tubular sodium reabsorption.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: hCG Role in Fetal Sex Differentiation
front: Explain the specific mechanism by which Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) affects the development of a male fetus.
back:
hCG mimics Luteinizing Hormone (LH):

- Stimulates fetal interstitial Leydig cells.
- Induces testosterone production.
- Triggers development of male sex organs.
- Promotes testicular descent into the scrotum near term.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Contrast the specific effects of Estrogen and Progesterone on breast development during pregnancy.
back:
Ducts vs Alveoli:

- Estrogen: Stimulates growth of the ductal system and stromal fat deposition.
- Progesterone: Promotes lobule-alveolar growth and develops secretory characteristics in alveolar cells.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Identify the primary source of 'Relaxin' during pregnancy and its effect on pelvic anatomy.
back:
Ovarian Corpus Luteum and Placenta.

- Relaxes and softens the ligaments of the symphysis pubis.
- Increases elasticity of the pelvic joints.
- Potentially aids in softening the cervix for delivery.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: During pregnancy, the maternal anterior pituitary gland enlarges by approximately 50%, while the secretion of [___] is almost totally suppressed.
back:
• Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing hormone (LH).
• Suppression occurs due to the potent inhibitory feedback of placental estrogens and progesterone.
• This prevents new follicle maturation during gestation.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A healthy 36-week pregnant woman presents with mild pedal edema and significantly increased blood volume. These physiological changes are partially mediated by a 2-fold increase in which adrenal hormone?
back:
• Aldosterone.
• It promotes renal sodium reabsorption and water retention.
• Levels peak at the end of gestation, contributing to maternal fluid expansion.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain the mechanism behind the increased production of thyroxine in the maternal thyroid gland during pregnancy.
back:
• The gland enlarges by ~50%.
• Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) exerts a thyrotropic effect.
• Small amounts of human chorionic thyrotropin from the placenta further stimulate thyroxine output.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the maternal parathyroid gland activity during pregnancy versus the lactation period.
back:
• Pregnancy: PTH increases to maintain maternal ECF calcium while fetal bones ossify.
• Lactation: PTH secretion is even higher than pregnancy.
• Reason: Growing infants require significantly more calcium via milk than fetuses.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Summarize the metabolic role of increased maternal glucocorticoid secretion during gestation.
back:
• Secretion increases moderately throughout pregnancy.
• Helps mobilize amino acids from maternal tissues.
• Provides essential protein substrates for fetal growth and tissue synthesis.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Although its levels rise steadily from the fifth week of pregnancy, the actual secretion of milk by [___] is inhibited by estrogen and progesterone until birth.
back:
• Prolactin.
• Placental steroids block its lactogenic effect during pregnancy.
• Postpartum loss of placental hormones allows milk production to commence.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: An infant born to an untreated diabetic mother exhibits macrosomia and severe neonatal hypoglycemia. This results from the compensatory hypertrophy of which fetal endocrine structure?
back:
• Islets of Langerhans (Beta cells).
• High maternal glucose triggers fetal insulin hypersecretion.
• Post-birth, high insulin levels cause rapid removal of the infant's blood glucose.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain why hypothalamic damage during pregnancy typically results in increased Prolactin levels while other anterior pituitary hormones decrease.
back:
• Prolactin is under tonic inhibition by hypothalamic Dopamine (Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone).
• Other pituitary hormones require hypothalamic releasing factors.
• Damage removes inhibition, leading to autonomous lactotrope secretion.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the typical increase in Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) with the average total weight gain in a normal pregnancy.
back:
• BMR: Increases by ~15% during the latter half of pregnancy.
• Weight Gain: Averages 25–35 pounds total.
• Weight includes fetus (~8lbs), fluid (~5lbs), and stored maternal fat.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Identify the three specific anterior pituitary hormones that show significantly increased secretion rates in the pregnant mother.
back:
• Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH).
• Thyrotropin (TSH).
• Prolactin.
• These increases support the higher metabolic demands and preparation for lactation.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: The specific glycoprotein secreted by syncytiotrophoblast cells that prevents the sloughing of the uterine endometrium after implantation is [___].
back:
* Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG).
* Maintains the corpus luteum and prevents its involution.
* Stimulates continued secretion of progesterone and estrogens by the ovary.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: A 28-year-old pregnant female undergoes an emergency surgical procedure at 6 weeks gestation. If the corpus luteum is accidentally removed, the pregnancy will likely terminate because the [___] has not yet assumed sufficient steroidogenic function.
back:
* Placenta.
* The placenta usually takes over major progesterone and estrogen production after the 7th to 12th week of gestation.
* Early removal of the corpus luteum leads to spontaneous abortion.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: Metabolic Role of Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS) alters maternal energy usage to prioritize fetal nutrition.
back:
* Induces maternal insulin resistance.
* Decreases maternal glucose utilization, increasing availability for the fetus.
* Stimulates lipolysis, mobilizing maternal free fatty acids as an alternative energy source for the mother.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Contrast the influence of placental Estrogen versus Progesterone on the development of gap junctions and uterine myometrial contractility.
back:
* Estrogen: Increases the number of gap junctions and enhances myometrial excitability/contractility.
* Progesterone: Inhibits gap junction formation and decreases uterine contractility to prevent spontaneous abortion.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Identify the primary steroid precursor, synthesized by fetal and maternal adrenal glands, that the placenta converts into estrogens.
back:
* Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA).
* The placenta lacks enzymes for de novo synthesis from cholesterol.
* Uses fetal/maternal androgens to produce estradiol, estrone, and estriol.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: The hormone [___] is responsible for promoting the development of decidual cells in the uterine endometrium, which are vital for early embryonic nutrition.
back:
* Progesterone.
* Converts stromal cells into nutrient-rich (glycogen/lipids) decidual cells.
* Essential for providing "uterine milk" before placental circulation is established.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: hCG Role in Male Fetal Development
front: A male neonate is born with female external genitalia. This failure of masculine differentiation in utero suggests a deficiency in the placental hormone [___], which normally stimulates fetal testosterone production.
back:
* Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG).
* Exerts an LH-like effect on fetal Leydig cells.
* Triggers testosterone secretion, inducing male sexual organ formation and testicular descent.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Describe the hormonal mechanism responsible for the maternal "diabetogenic" state observed in the latter half of pregnancy.
back:
* Mediated primarily by Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS).
* hCS antagonizes insulin action in the mother.
* Results in mild maternal hyperglycemia, ensuring a continuous glucose gradient for fetal growth.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: Hormonal Inhibition of Lactation During Pregnancy
front: Contrast the functional effects of Progesterone and Prolactin on the mammary glands during the gestational period.
back:
* Progesterone: Stimulates lobule-alveolar growth but actively inhibits milk secretion.
* Prolactin: Promotes milk synthesis, but its secretagogue effect is suppressed by high estrogen/progesterone until birth.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Name the specific hormone, secreted by both the corpus luteum and placenta, that acts as a vasodilator and softens the cervix for delivery.
back:
* Relaxin.
* Relaxes the ligaments of the symphysis pubis.
* Contributes to increased renal blood flow and cardiac output during pregnancy.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: The placental hormone primarily responsible for preventing the involution of the corpus luteum and preventing menstruation in early pregnancy is [___].
back:
• Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
• Secreted by syncytial trophoblast cells
• Stimulates corpus luteum to secrete large amounts of progesterone and estrogens
• Detectable in blood 8–9 days after ovulation

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: Metabolic Effects of Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin
front: A 28-year-old female at 30 weeks gestation shows reduced insulin sensitivity and elevated blood glucose. This physiological metabolic shift is primarily driven by [___].
back:
• Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS)
• Also known as Human Placental Lactogen
• Decreases maternal glucose utilization to prioritize fetal supply
• Promotes lipolysis, releasing free fatty acids for maternal energy

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Describe the biological mechanism by which the placenta produces large quantities of estrogens despite lacking the enzymes for de novo synthesis from cholesterol.
back:
• Uses androgenic precursors (DHEA and 16-hydroxy-DHEA)
• Precursors are synthesized in maternal and fetal adrenal glands
• Trophoblast cells convert these weak androgens into estradiol, estrone, and estriol

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Contrast the secretion patterns of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) and placental Progesterone throughout the duration of a normal pregnancy.
back:
• hCG: Peaks at 10–12 weeks; declines and plateaus by 16–20 weeks
• Progesterone: Increases progressively and linearly until parturition
• Placenta takes over progesterone production from corpus luteum after 7–12 weeks

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Identify the specific effect of placental progesterone on the uterine myometrium and its significance in maintaining pregnancy.
back:
• Decreases myometrial contractility
• Reduces the frequency and intensity of uterine contractions
• Prevents spontaneous abortion by maintaining a quiescent uterine environment

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Estrogens secreted during pregnancy cause the [___] joints to become relatively limber and the symphysis pubis to become elastic to facilitate delivery.
back:
• Sacroiliac joints
• Allows the pelvic ligaments to relax
• Facilitates easier passage of the fetus through the birth canal

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: A pregnant patient exhibits mild signs of thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism). Explain the hormonal cross-reactivity responsible for this physiological finding.
back:
• hCG has weak thyrotropic activity
• Placenta also secretes 'human chorionic thyrotropin'
• Results in maternal thyroid gland enlargement (50%) and increased thyroxine production

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Explain the role of the 'fetal zone' of the fetal adrenal cortex in supporting placental steroidogenesis.
back:
• Constitutes 80% of the fetal adrenal cortex
• Primary function is to secrete dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)
• DHEA serves as the mandatory substrate for placental estrogen production

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Contrast the primary developmental roles of Estrogen and Progesterone on the maternal breasts during pregnancy.
back:
• Estrogen: Stimulates ductal growth and stroma/fat deposition
• Progesterone: Stimulates lobule-alveolar system development (budding of alveoli)
• Both hormones inhibit actual milk secretion until after parturition

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Which specific hormone is responsible for stimulating the descent of the testes in the male fetus near the end of pregnancy?
back:
• Testosterone
• Secretion is stimulated by Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) acting on fetal Leydig cells
• Critical for male sexual organ differentiation during intrauterine life

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: During pregnancy, the maternal anterior pituitary gland undergoes significant hypertrophy, increasing its overall size by approximately [___] percent.
back:
• 50%
• Increases production of ACTH, TSH, and Prolactin
• Functions to meet the increased metabolic load of the mother and fetus.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A pregnant woman maintains normal serum calcium levels despite the fetus rapidly removing calcium for skeletal ossification. Identify the non-placental endocrine response responsible for this stability.
back:
• Hypertrophy of the maternal parathyroid glands
• Increased secretion of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
• Stimulates calcium absorption from maternal bone to maintain extracellular fluid levels.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain the mechanism by which the maternal ovaries are prevented from initiating new follicular growth during gestation.
back:
• Placental estrogens and progesterone exert strong negative feedback
• This feedback almost totally suppresses maternal FSH and LH secretion
• Prevents the onset of new ovarian cycles during pregnancy.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the maternal adrenal cortex activity in the third trimester with that of a non-pregnant state regarding aldosterone and sodium handling.
back:
• Aldosterone increases 2-fold, peaking at term
• Non-pregnant state has lower basal levels
• Pregnancy change promotes excessive renal sodium and water reabsorption, leading to fluid retention.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Identify the non-placental source of Relaxin and its primary anatomical targets in the early stages of pregnancy.
back:
• Secreted by the ovarian corpus luteum
• Stimulated by hCG
• Targets pelvic ligaments (sacroiliac joints/symphysis pubis) for relaxation and softens the cervix.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: To support increased metabolic demands, the maternal thyroid gland typically enlarges and increases thyroxine production by [___] percent.
back:
• 50%
• Enlargement results in a higher basal metabolic rate
• Driven by placental thyrotropic factors and increased hormone synthesis.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A pregnant patient exhibits moderately elevated plasma cortisol. What is the specific metabolic utility of this glucocorticoid increase for the developing fetus?
back:
• Mobilization of amino acids from maternal tissues
• Provides substrates for fetal tissue synthesis
• Helps manage the increased metabolic load on the mother.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Describe the dual pathway by which the maternal thyroid gland is stimulated by the placenta during a normal pregnancy.
back:
• Thyrotropic effect of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
• Secretion of Human Chorionic Thyrotropin from the placenta
• Both stimulate the thyroid to increase thyroxine production.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Distinguish between the changes in maternal ACTH and FSH secretion levels during the second trimester of pregnancy.
back:
• ACTH: Secretion increases to mobilize amino acids for the fetus
• FSH: Secretion is almost totally suppressed by placental steroids
• Prevents follicular maturation while supporting protein anabolism.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Specify the average percentage increase in the maternal basal metabolic rate (BMR) during the latter half of pregnancy.
back:
• 15% increase
• Caused by increased thyroxine, adrenocortical, and sex hormone secretion
• Often leads to sensations of being overheated in the mother.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: During pregnancy, the maternal anterior pituitary gland undergoes significant hypertrophy, increasing in size by approximately [___] percent.
back:
* 50%
* Results in increased production of ACTH, TSH, and Prolactin
* FSH and LH are suppressed by placental steroids

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A 28-week pregnant female presents with a non-tender enlargement of the thyroid gland. Lab tests show elevated total thyroxine (T4). Identify the non-placental hormonal driver and the placental factor responsible.
back:
* Driver: Maternal Thyroid Gland (enlarges ~50%)
* Factors: Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) and Human Chorionic Thyrotropin
* Both placental factors mimic TSH to stimulate thyroxine production

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain the mechanism by which pregnancy results in the near-total suppression of maternal follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH) secretion.
back:
* High levels of placental estrogens and progesterone
* Potent negative feedback on the anterior pituitary
* Prevents the development of new ovarian follicles during gestation

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the physiological state of the maternal parathyroid glands in a woman with a high-calcium diet versus one with a calcium-deficient diet during pregnancy.
back:
* High-calcium: Normal maternal gland activity
* Calcium-deficient: Gland hypertrophy and increased PTH secretion
* Mechanism: PTH mobilizes maternal bone stores to meet fetal ossification demands

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Identify the specific non-placental mineralocorticoid that increases two-fold during pregnancy and its primary effect on maternal hemodynamics.
back:
* Hormone: Aldosterone
* Increases renal sodium reabsorption
* Works with estrogens to cause fluid retention and expand maternal blood volume

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: The hormone [___], primarily secreted by the corpus luteum and placenta, contributes to the softening of the uterine cervix and relaxation of pelvic ligaments.
back:
* Relaxin
* Weakens/relaxes the symphysis pubis
* Acts as a vasodilator to increase cardiac output and renal blood flow

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A pregnant patient exhibits elevated plasma cortisol levels. Explain the physiological benefit of this glucocorticoid increase for the developing fetus.
back:
* Mobilizes amino acids from maternal tissues
* Provides building blocks for synthesis of fetal proteins and tissues
* Helps manage the increased maternal metabolic load

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which the maternal thyroid gland maintains increased activity despite the feedback loops of pregnancy.
back:
* hCG and human chorionic thyrotropin (placental) act as TSH agonists
* Direct stimulation of maternal thyroid follicles
* Supports the ~15% increase in maternal basal metabolic rate (BMR)

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the secretory patterns of Prolactin versus Gonadotropins (FSH/LH) from the maternal anterior pituitary during pregnancy.
back:
* Prolactin: Rises steadily from 5th week to term (10-20x normal)
* FSH/LH: Almost totally suppressed throughout pregnancy
* Prolactin is promoted by the pituitary; gonadotropins are inhibited by placental steroids

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Which maternal endocrine gland undergoes the most significant hypertrophy to handle the increased demand for ACTH, TSH, and Prolactin during gestation?
back:
* Anterior Pituitary Gland
* Enlarges by approximately 50%
* This change is necessary to support fetal growth and prepare for lactation

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: To prevent the termination of pregnancy shortly after implantation, the syncytial trophoblast cells secrete [___] to maintain the viability of the corpus luteum.
back:
• Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG).
• Prevents involution of the corpus luteum.
• Stimulates the corpus luteum to secrete large quantities of progesterone and estrogens.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: A pregnant woman in her third trimester develops decreased insulin sensitivity and elevated plasma free fatty acids. The placental hormone primarily responsible for these metabolic shifts is [___].
back:
• Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS).
• Decreases maternal glucose utilization to ensure fetal glucose availability.
• Promotes maternal fat mobilization as an alternative energy source.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Explain the specific mechanism by which placental progesterone supports the early structural integrity of pregnancy within the uterus.
back:
• Converts endometrial stromal cells into nutrient-rich decidual cells.
• Inhibits uterine smooth muscle contractility to prevent spontaneous abortion.
• Increases fallopian tube secretions to nourish the morula/blastocyst.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: hCG vs LH in Fetal Sex Differentiation
front: Contrast Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH) regarding their origin and specific roles in male fetal development.
back:
• Origin: hCG is placental (syncytial trophoblasts); LH is pituitary.
• Role: hCG stimulates fetal Leydig cells to produce testosterone.
• Effect: Ensures the differentiation of male sexual organs and testicular descent.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Describe the anatomical and functional changes in the maternal anterior pituitary gland during pregnancy.
back:
• Enlarges by at least 50%.
• Increases production of ACTH, TSH, and Prolactin.
• FSH and LH are suppressed by placental estrogen and progesterone.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: During the final months of pregnancy, the 2-fold increase in maternal [___] secretion, coupled with high estrogen levels, leads to significant sodium and water retention.
back:
• Aldosterone.
• Promotes renal sodium reabsorption.
• Contributes to the 30% increase in maternal blood volume.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: A lactating mother complains of muscle cramps; labs show normal plasma calcium. Explain the hormonal adjustment that prevents hypocalcemia despite high calcium loss in milk.
back:
• Hypertrophy of maternal parathyroid glands.
• Increased Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) secretion.
• Stimulates maternal bone resorption to maintain calcium homeostasis.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Explain how the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio shift after the seventh month of pregnancy prepares the uterus for labor.
back:
• Estrogens increase gap junctions between myometrial smooth muscle cells.
• Upregulates oxytocin receptors on the uterine wall.
• Estrogen dominance overrides the 'progesterone block' to increase contractility.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Contrast the roles of placental estrogens and Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS) in maternal breast development.
back:
• Estrogens: Stimulate growth and branching of the ductal system and stromal fat deposition.
• hCS: Exerts lactogenic properties and protein anabolic effects to support breast preparation.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Identify the primary non-reproductive physiological roles of Relaxin during pregnancy.
back:
• Acts as a vasodilator to increase renal blood flow.
• Increases maternal venous return and cardiac output.
• Softens the uterine cervix for delivery.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: The specific placental cells responsible for the secretion of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) into the maternal circulation are the [___].
back:
• Syncytiotrophoblast cells.
• Secretion begins 8–9 days post-ovulation.
• Levels peak at 10–12 weeks of gestation.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: A 28-week pregnant female develops mild hyperglycemia. This 'diabetogenic' effect of pregnancy is primarily driven by [___], which decreases maternal insulin sensitivity to prioritize glucose for the fetus.
back:
• Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS).
• Also known as Human Placental Lactogen (hPL).
• Increases maternal free fatty acid mobilization for energy.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Explain the primary biological role of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) regarding the maintenance of the early pregnancy.
back:
• Prevents involution of the corpus luteum.
• Stimulates corpus luteum to secrete high levels of progesterone/estrogen.
• Maintains the decidual nature of the endometrium for implantation.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
coreConcept: Placental Gas Exchange and Bohr Effect
front: Contrast the direction of the Bohr effect in maternal versus fetal blood at the placental interface (Double Bohr Effect).
back:
• Maternal blood: CO2 uptake from fetus makes it acidic, shifting curve right to release O2.
• Fetal blood: CO2 loss to mother makes it alkaline, shifting curve left to bind O2.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Identify the source and nature of the steroid precursors used by the placenta to synthesize its high levels of estrogens.
back:
• Source: Maternal and fetal adrenal glands.
• Precursor: Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and 16-hydroxy-DHEA.
• Mechanism: Placenta converts these weak androgens into estradiol, estrone, and estriol.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: The placental hormone essential for preventing spontaneous abortion by decreasing the frequency and intensity of uterine contractions is [___].
back:
• Progesterone.
• Develops decidual cells for embryo nutrition.
• Increases fallopian tube secretions before implantation.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: In a male fetus, Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) serves a critical developmental function by stimulating [___] to produce testosterone.
back:
• Fetal interstitial cells of Leydig.
• Testosterone is required for male sex organ differentiation.
• Also triggers descent of testes into the scrotum near term.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Describe the hormonal mechanism by which the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio initiates parturition near the end of pregnancy.
back:
• Progesterone (inhibitory) levels plateau or fall slightly.
• Estrogens (stimulatory) continue to rise after month seven.
• High ratio increases gap junctions and oxytocin receptors in myometrium.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: Contrast the physiological roles of Relaxin and Estrogens in preparing the maternal pelvis for delivery.
back:
• Relaxin: Softens the uterine cervix and serves as a systemic vasodilator.
• Estrogens: Specifically relax pelvic ligaments (sacroiliac and symphysis pubis) for fetal passage.

category: Explain the hormonal factors in pregnancy/ hormones of placenta
front: State the timing of the peak concentration of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) during a normal pregnancy.
back:
• Peak: 10 to 12 weeks of gestation.
• Low plateau: Occurs by 16 to 20 weeks.
• Remains at lower levels until parturition.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: The maternal anterior pituitary gland typically enlarges by [___]% during a normal pregnancy to meet the increased metabolic demands of the mother and fetus.
back:
50%
* It increases its production of ACTH, TSH, and Prolactin.
* Secretion of FSH and LH is conversely suppressed to nearly zero.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A woman in her third trimester exhibits physiological edema and a 30% increase in blood volume. The non-placental mineralocorticoid primarily responsible for this fluid retention is [___].
back:
Aldosterone
* Secretion increases 2-fold, reaching a peak at the end of gestation.
* Functions to increase renal sodium and water reabsorption to expand maternal blood volume.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which maternal Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH) are suppressed during pregnancy.
back:
Negative Feedback Loop:
* Tremendous quantities of placental Estrogen and Progesterone inhibit the anterior pituitary.
* This suppression prevents the initiation of new ovarian cycles during gestation.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the physiological changes in maternal ACTH versus FSH secretion during a normal pregnancy.
back:
ACTH: Increases significantly to stimulate glucocorticoids for maternal nutrient mobilization.
* FSH: Is almost totally suppressed by high placental steroid levels to prevent ovulation.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Identify the non-placental hormone secreted by the corpus luteum that aids in softening the cervix and relaxing pelvic ligaments.
back:
Relaxin
* Polypeptide that facilitates the expansion of the sacroiliac and symphysis pubis joints.
* Acts as a vasodilator, contributing to increased renal blood flow and cardiac output.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Maternal thyroid function increases by 50% during pregnancy due to the thyrotropic activity of the placental hormone [___].
back:
Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
* hCG has weak thyrotropic effects that increase thyroxine (T4) production.
* The maternal thyroid gland enlarges physically to support the increased metabolic rate.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A 28-week pregnant woman with poor dietary calcium intake shows progressive decalcification of her bones. This compensatory maternal state is driven by an increase in [___].
back:
Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
* Maternal parathyroid glands enlarge to maintain extracellular calcium levels.
* Promotes bone resorption to provide calcium for fetal skeletal ossification.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain the role of increased maternal glucocorticoid secretion (Cortisol) during the course of pregnancy.
back:
Metabolic Support:
* Mobilizes amino acids from maternal tissues for fetal protein synthesis.
* Contributes to the insulin-resistant state of pregnancy to prioritize fetal glucose supply.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the physical enlargement and hormonal output of the maternal pituitary gland versus the thyroid gland during pregnancy.
back:
Pituitary: Enlarges by 50%; increases ACTH, TSH, and Prolactin while suppressing LH/FSH.
* Thyroid: Enlarges by 50%; increases thyroxine output via thyrotropic stimulation from placental hCG.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Describe the timing and source of the 10- to 20-fold surge in Prolactin observed at the end of pregnancy.
back:
Maternal Anterior Pituitary:
* Levels rise steadily from the 5th week of gestation until birth.
* Prepares the mammary glands for lactation, though milk secretion is inhibited by placental steroids.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: The maternal cardiac output typically reaches a peak of 30% to 40% above normal levels by the [___] week of gestation.
back:
• 27th week of pregnancy.
• It may slightly decrease during the final 8 weeks despite high uterine blood flow.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A 34-week pregnant female presents with sudden weight gain, edema, and a blood pressure of 155/105 mmHg. This condition is primarily initiated by [___].
back:
• Insufficient placental blood supply (ischemia).
• Failure of trophoblasts to adequately remodel maternal spiral arteries.
• Release of antiangiogenic factors (s-Flt1 and endoglin).

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Explain the physiological basis for the 50% increase in maternal Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) during a normal pregnancy.
back:
• Renal vasodilation mediated by nitric oxide or relaxin.
• Compensatory response to increased tubular reabsorption of salt and water.
• Increased overall blood volume.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the approximate weight of the uterus in a non-pregnant state with its weight at full-term pregnancy.
back:
• Non-pregnant: ~50 grams.
• Full-term: ~1100 grams.
• This represents a 22-fold increase in muscle mass.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Identify the primary anatomical change in the maternal skeletal system induced by estrogens to facilitate the passage of the fetus through the birth canal.
back:
• Relaxation of the pelvic ligaments.
• Increased elasticity of the symphysis pubis.
• Limbering of the sacroiliac joints.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: To avoid hypochromic anemia, a pregnant woman requires a total of approximately [___] mg of extra iron for the fetus and her own expanded blood volume.
back:
• 975 mg total.
• 375 mg for the fetus and 600 mg for the mother's extra blood.
• Maternal iron stores are often insufficient (typically <700 mg).

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A patient in her third trimester frequently complains of feeling 'overheated' and requiring extra snacks between meals. These symptoms result from [___].
back:
• 15% increase in Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR).
• High levels of thyroxine and adrenocortical hormones.
• Increased metabolic load of the fetus and expanded maternal organs.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Describe the mechanism by which the maternal body maintains normal plasma calcium levels despite the fetus removing calcium to ossify its bones.
back:
• Hypertrophy of maternal parathyroid glands.
• Increased Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) secretion.
• Stimulation of calcium absorption from the mother's bones and gastrointestinal tract.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the magnitude of the increase in maternal blood volume versus maternal oxygen consumption at the time of term.
back:
• Blood Volume: ~30% increase (1–2 liters).
• Oxygen Consumption: ~20% increase.
• The volume expansion provides a safety factor for delivery-related blood loss.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Identify the average replacement intervals for water and electrolytes within the amniotic fluid during pregnancy.
back:
• Water: Replaced every 3 hours.
• Electrolytes (Na and K): Replaced every 15 hours.
• Much of the fluid is derived from fetal renal excretion.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Uterine contractility is enhanced near term because [___] increases the number of gap junctions between adjacent smooth muscle cells.
back:
• Estrogen.
• Promotes electrical coupling between myocytes.
• Increases rhythmic synchrony of contractions to facilitate effective labor.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: A patient with a twin pregnancy is noted to go into labor 19 days earlier than the average singleton pregnancy. This phenomenon is primarily attributed to the mechanical factor of [___].
back:
• Uterine stretch.
• Mechanical stretching of smooth muscle naturally increases its contractility.
• Intermittent stretch from fetal movements also increases excitability.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Explain the "Ferguson Reflex" and its role in the positive feedback loop of labor.
back:
• Cervical stretch/irritation triggers neurogenic signals to the hypothalamus.
• Results in increased oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary.
• Oxytocin induces stronger contractions, further stretching the cervix.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast the effects of progesterone and estrogen on the myometrium during the final month of gestation.
back:
• Progesterone: Inhibits contractility to maintain uterine quiescence.
• Estrogen: Increases contractility by upregulating oxytocin receptors.
• Near term, the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio increases significantly.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Identify the local chemical factors released by fetal membranes that act as powerful stimulants for uterine contractions during labor.
back:
• Prostaglandins.
• Released in high concentrations during labor.
• Directly increase the intensity of myometrial contractions and cervical ripening.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: During the second stage of labor, the uterine contractions are supplemented by neurogenic reflexes that cause intense contractions of the [___] muscles.
back:
• Abdominal muscles.
• Triggered by pain signals from the birth canal.
• Adds significant downward force to aid fetal expulsion.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
coreConcept: Cervical Irritation as a Labor Trigger
front: An obstetrician ruptures the fetal membranes to "induce labor" in a patient. Describe the physiological basis for why this procedure initiates uterine contractions.
back:
• The fetal head stretches the cervix more forcefully.
• Initiates the positive feedback cycle of labor contractions.
• Triggers both myogenic and neurogenic reflexes to the fundus.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: How does the change in myometrial oxytocin receptors contribute to the onset of parturition?
back:
• Receptor density increases drastically in the final months.
• Enhances uterine responsiveness to existing oxytocin levels.
• Allows weak rhythmic contractions to transition into strong labor.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Distinguish between Braxton Hicks contractions and true labor contractions regarding their physiological progression.
back:
• Braxton Hicks: Weak, slow, and non-progressive rhythmic contractions.
• Labor: Strong, self-intensifying contractions driven by positive feedback.
• Labor contractions progressively stretch the cervix until delivery.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Name two hormones secreted by the fetus itself that may participate in initiating uterine contractions.
back:
• Fetal Oxytocin (from fetal pituitary).
• Fetal Cortisol (from fetal adrenal glands).
• Both substances stimulate the myometrium directly or indirectly via prostaglandins.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: During the later stages of pregnancy, maternal minute ventilation increases by approximately [___] percent, largely due to progesterone increasing the sensitivity of the respiratory center to carbon dioxide.
back:
• 50% increase.
• Leads to a decrease in arterial PCO2.
• Oxygen consumption also increases by ~20% due to maternal size and increased BMR.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A pregnant woman at 30 weeks gestation presents with a hemoglobin of 11 g/dL, despite a 20% increase in her total red cell mass. Identify the underlying physiological phenomenon.
back:
• Physiological anemia of pregnancy.
• Maternal blood volume increases by ~30%.
• Plasma volume increases more than red cell mass, causing hemodilution.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Explain the physiological mechanism behind the 50% increase in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) observed during a normal pregnancy.
back:
• Renal vasodilation mediated by nitric oxide or relaxin.
• Significant increase in renal blood flow.
• Acts as compensation for increased tubular reabsorption of salt and water.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the remodeling of maternal spiral arteries in a normal pregnancy versus a pregnancy complicated by preeclampsia.
back:
• Normal: Trophoblasts convert spiral arteries into large, low-resistance, high-flow vessels.
• Preeclampsia: Trophoblasts fail to invade adequately; vessels remain narrow, leading to placental ischemia.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Describe the maternal parathyroid gland's response to the calcium demands of fetal skeletal ossification.
back:
• Glands enlarge (hypertrophy) significantly.
• Increased PTH secretion promotes calcium absorption from maternal bones.
• Effect is even more pronounced during lactation.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Of the average 25 to 35 pounds gained during a normal pregnancy, the fetus itself accounts for approximately [___] pounds.
back:
• 8 pounds.
• Amniotic fluid, placenta, and membranes add ~4 pounds.
• Remainder is uterine/breast growth (~5 lbs), extra fluid, and fat.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A woman in her second trimester experiences a 15% increase in her basal metabolic rate (BMR). Identify the hormonal changes and physical sensations associated with this shift.
back:
• Increased thyroxine, adrenocortical, and sex hormones.
• Patient frequently feels overheated (increased heat production).
• Higher energy expenditure required for muscle activity.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Explain how Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin (hCS) alters maternal carbohydrate metabolism to ensure fetal nutrition.
back:
• Decreases maternal insulin sensitivity.
• Reduces maternal glucose utilization, making more glucose available for the fetus.
• Promotes release of maternal free fatty acids for energy.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the maternal cardiac output at the 27th week of pregnancy with that of the final 8 weeks of gestation.
back:
• 27th Week: Peaks at 30% to 40% above normal.
• Final 8 Weeks: Falls to only slightly above normal (unexplained).
• Placental blood flow at term is ~625 ml/min.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Identify the primary source and turnover rate of the water in amniotic fluid.
back:
• Source: Mainly fetal renal excretion (urine).
• Turnover: Water is replaced once every 3 hours.
• Electrolytes (Na/K) are replaced every 15 hours.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: During pregnancy, the maternal anterior pituitary gland enlarges by at least [___]% to meet the increased metabolic demands of gestation.
back:
• 50%
• Increases production of ACTH, TSH, and Prolactin
• Gonadotropins (FSH and LH) are simultaneously suppressed.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A 26-year-old pregnant female has nearly undetectable laboratory levels of Follicle-Stimulating Hormone (FSH) and Luteinizing Hormone (LH). Explain the physiological basis for this finding.
back:
• High concentrations of placental estrogens and progesterone
• Direct inhibitory feedback on the anterior pituitary gland
• Prevents the initiation of new ovarian cycles during pregnancy.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Explain the biological mechanisms that cause the maternal thyroid gland to increase thyroxine production by 50% during pregnancy.
back:
• Enlargement of the gland (50%)
• Thyrotropic effect of Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)
• Secretion of human chorionic thyrotropin by the placenta.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the maternal roles and changes of glucocorticoids versus aldosterone during the course of a normal pregnancy.
back:
• Glucocorticoids: Moderate increase; mobilize maternal amino acids for fetal tissue synthesis.
• Aldosterone: Two-fold increase; promotes renal sodium reabsorption and contributes to expanded blood volume.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
coreConcept: Parathyroid Adaptation to Fetal Calcium Demand
front: Explain why the maternal parathyroid glands typically enlarge, particularly during the period of lactation.
back:
• Maintains normal maternal extracellular calcium levels
• Compensates for fetal calcium removal for bone ossification
• Sustains high calcium requirements for milk formation after delivery.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Maternal prolactin levels rise steadily from the fifth week of pregnancy until birth, reaching a peak concentration [___] times higher than nonpregnant levels.
back:
• 10 to 20
• Secreted by the anterior pituitary
• Promoted by placental human chorionic somatomammotropin despite estrogenic inhibition of actual milk secretion.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: A healthy pregnant woman presents with significant fluid retention and a 30% increase in blood volume by term. Aside from estrogen, identify the non-placental steroid most responsible for this effect.
back:
• Aldosterone
• Levels increase 2-fold toward the end of gestation
• Stimulates renal tubules to reabsorb excess sodium and water.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Describe the physiological mechanisms through which the hormone Relaxin facilitates the maternal response to pregnancy and labor.
back:
• Softens and dilates the cervix during delivery
• Relaxes pelvic ligaments (sacroiliac and symphysis pubis)
• Functions as a vasodilator to increase venous return and cardiac output.
