category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Contrast the changes in the anterior pituitary's 'metabolic' hormones (ACTH, TSH, Prolactin) with its 'gonadotropic' hormones (FSH, LH) during pregnancy.
back:
• Metabolic group: Production increases significantly (50%+) to support maternal-fetal metabolic load.
• Gonadotropic group: Production is almost totally suppressed by placental steroid negative feedback.

category: Explain the changes in non- placental hormones during pregnancy
front: Identify the three primary non-placental hormone classes responsible for the 15% increase in maternal Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) during late pregnancy.
back:
• Increased Thyroxine (Thyroid)
• Increased Glucocorticoids (Adrenal Cortex)
• Increased Sex Hormones (Estrogen and Progesterone).

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
coreConcept: Maternal Basal Metabolic Rate in Pregnancy
front: In the latter half of pregnancy, the mother's basal metabolic rate (BMR) typically increases by approximately [___] percent.
back:
• 15%
• Results in sensations of overheating
• Driven by increased secretion of thyroxine, adrenocortical hormones, and sex hormones

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A woman in her third trimester presents with fatigue and a CBC showing microcytic, hypochromic anemia. This condition often arises because the mother requires [___] mg of iron for her own blood expansion and [___] mg for the fetus.
back:
• 600 mg (Mother)
• 375 mg (Fetus)
• Total iron requirement often exceeds maternal stores, necessitating supplementation

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which progesterone alters maternal respiratory dynamics during pregnancy.
back:
• Increases respiratory center sensitivity to CO2
• Results in a 50% increase in minute ventilation
• Leads to a slight decrease in arterial PCO2 compared to non-pregnant states

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the peak timing and magnitude of the increase in maternal cardiac output versus maternal blood volume.
back:
• Cardiac Output: Increases 30%–40% above normal, peaking around the 27th week
• Blood Volume: Increases ~30% (1–2 liters), reaching its maximum shortly before term

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: During pregnancy, the maternal anterior pituitary gland enlarges by at least 50%. Identify the two hormones whose secretion is almost totally suppressed during this time.
back:
• Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
• Luteinizing hormone (LH)
• Suppression is caused by inhibitory feedback from placental estrogens and progesterone

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: In a normal pregnancy, the maternal renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) increase by approximately [___] percent.
back:
• 50%
• Result of renal vasodilation
• Likely mediated by nitric oxide or the hormone relaxin

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A 34-week pregnant female presents with hypertension and proteinuria. Pathophysiological evidence suggests this condition is initiated by [___] leading to the release of antiangiogenic factors.
back:
• Placental ischemia (insufficient blood supply)
• Release of s-Flt1 and soluble endoglin
• Causes widespread maternal vascular endothelial dysfunction and arterial spasm

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Describe the compensatory response of the maternal parathyroid glands to the demands of the developing fetus.
back:
• Glands enlarge to increase PTH secretion
• Promotes calcium absorption from maternal bones
• Maintains normal maternal extracellular calcium while the fetus removes calcium for skeletal ossification

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the maternal minute ventilation increase with the total oxygen consumption increase at term.
back:
• Minute Ventilation: Increases by ~50%
• Oxygen Consumption: Increases by ~20%
• This mismatch ensures adequate oxygenation but results in a relative state of maternal hypocapnia

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Identify the primary adrenal steroid that increases twofold by the end of pregnancy to facilitate maternal fluid retention.
back:
• Aldosterone
• Works alongside estrogens to increase renal sodium and water reabsorption
• Contributes to the expansion of maternal blood volume

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Near term, uterine contractility increases significantly because the ratio of [___] to [___] in the maternal plasma rises.
back:
• Estrogen; Progesterone
• Estrogen increases gap junctions and contractility.
• Progesterone, which inhibits uterine motility, remains constant or decreases.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in labor experiences stronger contractions as the fetal head descends and distends the cervix. Identify the specific neurogenic reflex and the hormone responsible for this positive feedback loop.
back:
• Ferguson Reflex
• Cervical stretch triggers oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary.
• Oxytocin further increases the strength of uterine fundic contractions.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which rising estrogen levels late in pregnancy facilitate synchronized myometrial contractions during labor.
back:
• Increases the number of gap junctions (connexins) between smooth muscle cells.
• Allows rapid electrical coupling across the uterus.
• Up-regulates oxytocin receptors in the myometrium.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
coreConcept: Braxton Hicks vs. True Labor Dynamics
front: Contrast the dynamics and progression of Braxton Hicks contractions with the intensely strong contractions observed during true labor.
back:
• Braxton Hicks: Weak, slow, rhythmic, non-progressive episodes.
• Labor Contractions: Driven by a self-reinforcing positive feedback loop.
• Labor contractions originate at the fundus and spread downward.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Identify three specific contributions from the fetus or fetal membranes that stimulate maternal uterine contractility.
back:
• Fetal posterior pituitary secretes oxytocin.
• Fetal adrenal glands secrete cortisol (a uterine stimulant).
• Fetal membranes release high concentrations of prostaglandins (PGE2 and PGF2α).

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: The clinical observation that twin pregnancies are delivered approximately 19 days earlier than singletons illustrates the role of [___] in increasing uterine contractility.
back:
• Mechanical Stretch
• Distension of smooth muscle increases its inherent contractility.
• Fetal movements also elicit intermittent myogenic contractions.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: During the induction of labor, a clinician administers a high-dose oxytocin infusion. Why must the resulting contractions remain intermittent to ensure fetal safety?
back:
• Continuous (spastic) contractions stop placental blood flow.
• Causes acute fetal hypoxia and distress.
• Intermittent contractions allow for fetal re-oxygenation between cycles.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Describe the specific intracellular and tissue-level roles of prostaglandins during the onset and progression of labor.
back:
• Directly stimulate myometrial smooth muscle contraction.
• Potentiate the contractile effects of oxytocin.
• Promote cervical "ripening" and softening for easier dilation.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast the intensity of contractions in the uterine fundus with those in the lower uterine segment during the expulsion stage of labor.
back:
• Fundus: High-intensity contractions to drive the fetus downward.
• Lower Segment: Weak contractions to allow passive stretching and passage.
• This gradient creates a wedge effect to dilate the cervix.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: In terms of feedback systems, explain why labor contractions proceed to completion while "false labor" contractions fade away.
back:
• True labor relies on a positive feedback loop with high gain.
• Each cycle must be stronger than the previous to sustain the loop.
• False labor lacks sufficient excitation, causing a retrograde decline.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: By the end of gestation, the maternal blood volume increases by approximately [___] percent, adding about 1 to 2 liters of extra blood to the circulatory system.
back:
• Approximately 30% increase
• Stimulated by aldosterone, estrogens, and fluid retention
• Provides a safety factor against blood loss during delivery

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A woman in her 3rd trimester presents with a 15% increase in basal metabolic rate and reports frequently feeling overheated. This specific shift in metabolic activity is driven by [___].
back:
• Increased secretion of thyroxine (+50%)
• Increased adrenocortical and sex hormones
• Metabolic load of the growing fetus

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Explain the specific mechanism by which progesterone alters maternal respiratory dynamics during pregnancy.
back:
• Increases minute ventilation by ~50%
• Enhances respiratory center sensitivity to carbon dioxide
• Results in a moderate decrease in arterial PCO2

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the renal hemodynamic changes (GFR and Blood Flow) seen in a healthy pregnant woman versus one diagnosed with preeclampsia.
back:
• Normal: RBF and GFR increase by ~50% due to vasodilation
• Preeclampsia: RBF and GFR decrease due to arterial spasm and endothelial dysfunction

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Describe the morphological and functional change in the maternal parathyroid glands in response to fetal calcium demands.
back:
• Glandular hypertrophy (enlargement)
• Increased secretion of Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)
• Mobilizes maternal bone calcium to facilitate fetal skeletal ossification

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: The maternal cardiac output increases to its maximum of [___] percent above normal by the 27th week of pregnancy.
back:
• 30 to 40 percent increase
• Driven by increased metabolism and high placental blood flow
• May decline slightly toward term for unknown reasons

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A patient at 34 weeks gestation presents with hypertension, proteinuria, and facial edema. The fundamental initiating event of this condition is thought to be [___].
back:
• Insufficient blood supply to the placenta (placental ischemia)
• Failure of trophoblastic cells to adequately remodel maternal uterine spiral arteries

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Explain the mechanism of the 'Double Bohr Effect' occurring at the placental interface to facilitate oxygen transport.
back:
• Fetal blood loses CO2, becoming alkaline (increasing O2 affinity)
• Maternal blood gains CO2, becoming acidic (decreasing O2 affinity)
• Both shifts favor oxygen movement from mother to fetus

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the effect of placental hormones on the maternal pituitary secretion of FSH/LH versus Prolactin.
back:
• FSH and LH: Almost totally suppressed via negative feedback from estrogens/progesterone
• Prolactin: Increases 10- to 20-fold, reaching peak at term

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Identify the three largest weight components that account for the average 25–35 pound weight gain in a normal pregnancy.
back:
• Fetus (~8 lbs)
• Amniotic fluid, placenta, and membranes (~4 lbs)
• Extra blood and extracellular fluid (~5 lbs)

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Uterine contractility is increased toward the end of pregnancy when the ratio of [___] to [___] rises significantly.
back:
• Estrogen; Progesterone.
• Estrogens increase gap junctions and excitability.
• Progesterone levels stay constant or decrease, removing its inhibitory effect on the myometrium.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: An obstetrician ruptures the membranes of a full-term patient to induce labor. Explain the primary mechanical stimulus this provides to initiate contractions.
back:
• Forceful engagement of the fetal head against the cervix.
• Mechanical stretch/irritation of the cervix.
• Initiates neurogenic reflexes (Ferguson Reflex) and myogenic transmission to increase fundal contractility.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Explain the role of prostaglandins in increasing the intensity of uterine contractions during labor.
back:
• Released in high concentrations by fetal membranes.
• Directly stimulate myometrial smooth muscle contraction.
• Synergize with oxytocin to convert weak rhythmicity into strong labor contractions.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast the physiological stimulus for oxytocin release in the Ferguson reflex with its stimulus in the milk-ejection reflex.
back:
• Ferguson Reflex: Triggered by mechanical stretching or irritation of the uterine cervix.
• Milk-ejection: Triggered by tactile suckling stimulus on the nipple.
• Both involve hypothalamic-posterior pituitary neurogenic pathways.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Name three fetal-derived hormonal factors that contribute to increased uterine contractility during parturition.
back:
• Fetal Oxytocin: Secreted by the fetal posterior pituitary.
• Fetal Cortisol: Secreted by the fetal adrenal glands.
• Prostaglandins: Released from the fetal membranes (amnion/chorion).

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: The neurogenic reflex where cervical stretching triggers posterior pituitary oxytocin release to further increase contractions is known as the [___] reflex.
back:
• Ferguson Reflex.
• It creates a positive feedback loop.
• Stretch leads to contraction, which causes further downward fetal thrust and more stretch.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: A patient carrying twins goes into labor 19 days earlier than a single-child pregnancy. Identify the primary mechanical factor responsible for this shortened gestation.
back:
• Excessive uterine musculature stretch.
• Stretching smooth muscle naturally increases its contractility.
• Twin-induced volume increase elicits earlier and stronger myogenic responses.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Explain the cellular mechanism by which estrogen increases the responsiveness of the myometrium to contractile stimuli near term.
back:
• Increases the number of gap junctions between adjacent smooth muscle cells.
• Up-regulates the expression of oxytocin receptors.
• Lowers the threshold for action potential propagation across the uterus.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast the pattern of uterine activity in Braxton Hicks contractions versus true labor contractions.
back:
• Braxton Hicks: Weak, slow, periodic rhythmic episodes throughout pregnancy.
• Labor Contractions: Intensely strong, frequent (every 1–3 minutes), following a self-reinforcing positive feedback loop.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Identify the posterior pituitary hormone that serves as the final common pathway for strong labor contractions and its receptors' status near term.
back:
• Oxytocin.
• Receptors on the uterine muscle increase significantly during the latter few months.
• This increases myometrial sensitivity to oxytocin levels.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Estrogen enhances uterine excitability near term by increasing the number of [___] between adjacent myometrial smooth muscle cells.
back:
• Gap junctions.
• These allow for rapid, coordinated myogenic transmission of electrical signals across the uterine wall.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: A woman carrying twins enters labor 19 days earlier than the typical 40-week gestation. This clinical finding highlights the mechanical factor of [___].
back:
• Uterine muscle stretch.
• Simply stretching smooth muscle increases its contractility and excitability.
• Fetal movements also elicit periodic contractions.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Explain the mechanism by which cervical stretching increases the rate of posterior pituitary hormone secretion during labor.
back:
• Initiates a neurogenic reflex (Ferguson reflex).
• Signals travel to the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei of the hypothalamus.
• Results in increased oxytocin release into circulation.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast the physiological effects of estrogen and progesterone on the myometrium during late pregnancy.
back:
• Estrogen: Increases excitability and contractility; rises from 7th month onward.
• Progesterone: Inhibits contractility to maintain quiescence; remains constant or decreases slightly.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Identify the primary chemical mediators released by fetal membranes that increase the intensity of uterine contractions.
back:
• Prostaglandins.
• Released in high concentrations at the time of labor to amplify contractile force.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: The fetal [___] glands contribute to uterine excitability near term by secreting large quantities of cortisol.
back:
• Adrenal glands.
• Fetal cortisol serves as a possible uterine stimulant alongside fetal pituitary oxytocin.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: A patient at term shows an 80-fold increase in uterine sensitivity to oxytocin compared to early pregnancy. This is pathophysiologically due to [___].
back:
• Upregulation of oxytocin receptors.
• Myometrial responsiveness to a given dose of oxytocin increases dramatically in the latter months.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Describe the positive feedback loop that suddenly converts slow Braxton Hicks contractions into strong labor contractions.
back:
• Cervical stretch excites fundic contraction.
• Fundic contraction pushes the baby downward.
• Downward thrust causes more cervical stretch and oxytocin release.
• Cycle repeats until expulsion.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast the intensity and location of uterine contractions at the start of labor versus the late second stage.
back:
• Start: Weak contractions every 30 minutes.
• Late Stage: Strong contractions every 1-3 minutes.
• Gradient: Strongest at the fundus; weak in the lower segment near the cervix.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Identify the trigger for the intense abdominal muscle contractions that assist the uterus during the second stage of labor.
back:
• Pain signals from the uterus and birth canal.
• Elicits neurogenic reflexes in the spinal cord.
• Results in forceful expulsion aid.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: From the seventh month of pregnancy onward, uterine excitability increases because [___] secretion continues to rise while [___] secretion remains constant or decreases.
back:
• 1. Estrogen
• 2. Progesterone
• This increased ratio facilitates myometrial contractility.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: A patient at 39 weeks gestation shows a significantly higher uterine sensitivity to a specific dose of oxytocin compared to earlier in the second trimester. The underlying pathophysiology involves [___].
back:
• Progressive upregulation of oxytocin receptors in the uterine muscle
• Increased receptor density during the final months of pregnancy.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Explain the specific physiological mechanism by which rising estrogen levels coordinate the smooth muscle cells of the uterus for labor.
back:
• Estrogen increases the number of gap junctions between adjacent myometrial cells
• This allows for rapid, synchronized electrical conduction and stronger contractions.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast Braxton Hicks contractions with labor contractions regarding their intensity and effect on the cervix.
back:
• Braxton Hicks: Weak, slow, and rhythmic; do not stretch the cervix.
• Labor: Exceptionally strong and progressive; cause cervical stretching and dilation.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Identify the local hormones released by fetal membranes in high concentrations during labor that act as potent uterine stimulants.
back:
• Prostaglandins
• These increase the intensity and frequency of uterine smooth muscle contractions.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: The neurogenic reflex where cervical stretching triggers the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin to further enhance labor is the [___].
back:
• Ferguson reflex
• This is a key component of the positive feedback loop of labor.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: A 34-week pregnant female with a twin gestation is likely to deliver significantly earlier than a patient with a singleton pregnancy. The primary mechanical factor responsible is [___].
back:
• Mechanical stretch of the uterine musculature
• Overstretching inherently increases smooth muscle contractility and excitability.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: How does the 'positive feedback theory' of labor explain the progression of contractions once the baby's head enters the birth canal?
back:
• 1. Head stretches cervix.
• 2. Stretch reflexively excites fundic contraction.
• 3. Contraction pushes head lower, increasing stretch.
• 4. Cycle repeats with increasing intensity.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Contrast the effects of fetal cortisol versus fetal oxytocin on the initiation of labor.
back:
• Fetal Cortisol: Secreted by fetal adrenals; acts as a potential uterine stimulant.
• Fetal Oxytocin: Secreted by fetal pituitary; directly excites uterine contractility.

category: Explain the mechanical and hormonal factors that increase uterine contractility during parturition
front: Identify the primary source and the trigger for the massive surge of maternal oxytocin seen during the second stage of labor.
back:
• Source: Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)
• Trigger: Stretching or irritation of the uterine cervix (neurogenic reflex).

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: During pregnancy, the hormone primarily responsible for the development of breast lobules and the budding of alveoli into secretory structures is [___].
back:
• Progesterone
• Acts synergistically with estrogen and other metabolic hormones
• Converts breasts into potentially milk-producing organs

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A nursing mother experiences milk flow while merely hearing her baby cry. Identify the underlying neuroendocrine reflex and the specific hormone responsible.
back:
• Milk ejection (let-down) reflex
• Mediated by Oxytocin
• Emotional signals to the hypothalamus trigger posterior pituitary release

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain why actual milk secretion is inhibited during pregnancy despite the 10- to 20-fold rise in maternal prolactin levels.
back:
• High levels of placental Estrogen and Progesterone suppress actual milk secretion
• These hormones inhibit the lactogenic effect of prolactin until after delivery

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the specific physiological roles of Prolactin and Oxytocin in the process of lactation.
back:
• Prolactin: Stimulates milk production and secretion into the mammary alveoli
• Oxytocin: Causes milk ejection (let-down) by contracting myoepithelial cells

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain the unique hypothalamic control of prolactin secretion compared to other anterior pituitary hormones.
back:
• Control is predominantly inhibitory
• Mediated by Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone (PIH), which is the catecholamine Dopamine
• Damage to the hypothalamus usually increases prolactin secretion

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The specialized fluid produced in the first few days postpartum, which contains high protein and lactose but lacks fat, is [___].
back:
• Colostrum
• Volume is 1/100th of later milk production
• Transition to copious milk occurs within 1-7 days

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A 26-year-old mother who is exclusively breastfeeding remains amenorrheic for several months. Explain the hormonal pathway responsible for this effect.
back:
• Suckling signals inhibit Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)
• This suppresses LH and FSH secretion
• Result: Inhibition of the ovarian cycle and ovulation

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Describe the physiological adaptation of the maternal parathyroid glands to the metabolic drain of calcium during heavy lactation.
back:
• Parathyroid glands enlarge (hypertrophy) significantly
• Stimulates bone decalcification to provide calcium for milk production
• Requires adequate maternal Vitamin D and Calcium intake

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the composition of human breast milk with cow's milk regarding the concentrations of lactose and protein.
back:
• Human Milk: Higher concentration of Lactose (approx. 50% more)
• Human Milk: Lower concentration of Protein (approx. 2-3 times less)

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Identify the specific cell type that contracts around mammary alveoli to express milk into the ductal system during the let-down reflex.
back:
• Myoepithelial cells
• Form a latticework surrounding the alveoli
• Contract in response to Oxytocin within 30-60 seconds

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The hormone primarily responsible for the growth and branching of the breast's ductal system during pregnancy is [___].
back:
Estrogen
- Stimulates ductile system growth
- Increases breast stroma
- Promotes fat deposition in breasts

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A 28-year-old female presents with galactorrhea following a traumatic head injury that severed the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels. Explain the physiological basis for her milk production.
back:
- Loss of Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone (PIH/Dopamine)
- Prolactin is uniquely under tonic inhibition by the hypothalamus
- Interruption of the portal system removes this inhibition, leading to hyperprolactinemia

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which suckling ensures the continuation of milk production for subsequent nursing periods.
back:
- Suckling stimulus triggers somatic sensory signals to the hypothalamus
- Induces a 10-to-20-fold surge in Prolactin from the anterior pituitary
- Prolactin stimulates alveolar cells to secrete milk for the next feed

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the fat content of colostrum with that of mature breast milk as described in the physiological text.
back:
- Colostrum: Produced in the first days after delivery; contains almost no fat
- Mature Milk: Copious secretion beginning 1-7 days postpartum; contains significant fat (approximately 3.3%)

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain why copious milk secretion is suppressed during pregnancy despite the presence of high prolactin levels.
back:
- Placental Estrogen and Progesterone inhibit the actual secretory action of prolactin on the alveoli
- High steroid levels promote breast development but block lactogenesis
- Sudden loss of these steroids postpartum allows prolactin to initiate lactation

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The milk let-down (ejection) process is physiologically mediated by the contraction of [___] cells surrounding the mammary alveoli.
back:
Myoepithelial cells
- Contraction is triggered by Oxytocin
- Generates a pressure of +10 to 20 mm Hg
- Forces milk from alveoli into the ductal system

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A nursing mother asks why her menstrual cycles have not returned 4 months after delivery. Explain the underlying neuroendocrine mechanism.
back:
- Suckling signals (or increased prolactin) inhibit hypothalamic GnRH release
- Suppresses anterior pituitary FSH and LH production
- Prevents the initiation of a new ovarian cycle (Lactational Amenorrhea)

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain the neuroendocrine reflex loop responsible for milk ejection within 1 minute of suckling.
back:
- Stimulus: Nipple suckling
- Afferent: Somatic nerves to hypothalamus
- Efferent: Posterior pituitary releases Oxytocin
- Target: Myoepithelial contraction in breast alveoli

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast human milk and cow's milk regarding their protein and lactose concentrations.
back:
- Human Milk: Higher lactose (6.8%) and lower protein (0.4-0.9%)
- Cow's Milk: Lower lactose (4.8%) and much higher protein (2.7-3.5%)

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Identify the specific hormone required to acting synergistically with estrogen to convert alveolar cells into a secretory state.
back:
Progesterone
- Promotes development of lobule-alveolar system
- Causes alveolar cells to proliferate and enlarge
- Establishes the secretory characteristics of breast tissue

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The specific hormone responsible for the "let-down" or milk ejection reflex by stimulating the contraction of myoepithelial cells is [___].
back:
• Oxytocin.
• Secreted by the posterior pituitary in response to suckling.
• Contracts myoepithelial cells to force milk from alveoli into the ductal system.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A postpartum woman has a hypothalamic lesion that prevents dopamine release into the hypophysial portal system. Predict the effect on milk production.
back:
• Lactation will increase or persist.
• Dopamine normally acts as the Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone (PIH).
• Absence of dopamine removes the tonic inhibition on anterior pituitary lactotropes, causing hyperprolactinemia.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which suckling maintains milk production and provides a natural contraceptive effect.
back:
• Prolactin Surges: Suckling triggers neurogenic signals for milk synthesis.
• GnRH Inhibition: Sensory signals inhibit hypothalamic GnRH release.
• FSH/LH Suppression: Low GnRH prevents the preovulatory LH surge, suppressing the ovarian cycle.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the structural roles of estrogen and progesterone in the development of the mammary glands during pregnancy.
back:
• Estrogen: Stimulates growth and branching of the ductal system and stromal fat deposition.
• Progesterone: Promotes the development of the lobule-alveolar system and secretory characteristics.
• Both: Synergistically inhibit actual milk secretion until delivery.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Justify why copious milk secretion only begins 1 to 7 days after parturition despite high prolactin levels during the third trimester.
back:
• Steroid Withdrawal: High placental estrogen and progesterone inhibit prolactin's effect on the breasts during pregnancy.
• Postpartum Drop: Delivery causes a sudden loss of these steroids.
• Initiation: Prolactin then assumes its natural milk-promoting role.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The thin, yellowish fluid secreted during the first few days after birth, containing high protein and lactose but almost no fat, is [___].
back:
• Colostrum.
• Provides essential antibodies and immune cells (neutrophils/macrophages).
• Volume is approximately 1/100 of subsequent mature milk production.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A nursing mother notices milk leaking from her nipples when she hears her infant crying. Explain the underlying physiological mechanism.
back:
• Emotional Milk Ejection: Psychic stimuli travel from the cortex to the hypothalamus.
• Oxytocin Release: Triggers the posterior pituitary without direct tactile nipple stimulation.
• Target: Contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the mammary alveoli.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain the skeletal consequences for a lactating mother who has an inadequate dietary intake of calcium and Vitamin D.
back:
• Calcium Drain: Milk production uses 2–3 grams of calcium daily.
• PTH Response: Parathyroid glands hypertrophy to maintain serum calcium.
• Bone Decalcification: PTH stimulates osteoclasts to mobilize maternal bone minerals for milk.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the functional differences between Prolactin and Oxytocin in the physiology of lactation.
back:
• Prolactin: Secreted by the anterior pituitary; promotes milk production/synthesis within the alveoli.
• Oxytocin: Secreted by the posterior pituitary; causes milk ejection (let-down) via myoepithelial contraction.
• Prolactin creates milk; Oxytocin delivers it.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Identify the metabolic substrates drained from the mother during peak lactation and the protective agents provided to the infant.
back:
• Substrates: Approximately 50g fat, 100g lactose, and significant calcium phosphate daily.
• Protective Agents: Antibodies (IgA), neutrophils, and macrophages.
• Specific Defense: Provides lethal protection against E. coli diarrhea.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: During pregnancy, the high levels of placental estrogens are primarily responsible for the growth and branching of the breast [___].
back:
• Ductal system
• Also involves stromal growth and fat deposition
• Requires permissive action of GH, cortisol, and insulin

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A pregnant woman exhibits high prolactin levels but does not secrete milk until after parturition. Identify the physiological mechanism preventing lactation during gestation.
back:
• Suppression by placental estrogen and progesterone
• These steroids inhibit prolactin's secretory effect on alveolar epithelium
• Postpartum withdrawal of these hormones allows lactation to begin

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain the role of oxytocin in the 'milk let-down' reflex upon the stimulus of suckling.
back:
• Suckling triggers oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary
• Oxytocin stimulates contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding alveoli
• This forces milk from the alveoli into the lactiferous ducts

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the physiological influences of Prolactin and Oxytocin on the lactating breast.
back:
• Prolactin: Promotes milk synthesis and secretion into the alveoli (production)
• Oxytocin: Causes milk ejection by contracting myoepithelial cells (delivery)
• Prolactin levels surge for ~1 hour postpartum during nursing

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Identify the primary hypothalamic factor that tonically inhibits prolactin and how suckling overrides this inhibition.
back:
• Dopamine (Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone)
• Suckling sends nervous signals to the hypothalamus to inhibit dopamine release
• Decreased dopamine allows the anterior pituitary to surge prolactin production

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: While estrogens develop the ductal system, the development of breast lobules and secretory alveoli specifically requires the hormone [___].
back:
• Progesterone
• Acts synergistically with estrogen and prolactin
• Converts the mammary gland into a functional secretory organ

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A nursing mother remains amenorrheic for several months after delivery. Describe the hormonal basis for this suppression of the ovarian cycle.
back:
• Suckling-induced prolactin surges inhibit hypothalamic GnRH secretion
• Suppressed GnRH leads to decreased pituitary FSH and LH
• This inhibits the preovulatory LH surge and subsequent ovulation

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Describe how the basal level of prolactin changes over time postpartum and its response to individual feeding episodes.
back:
• Basal prolactin returns to non-pregnant levels within weeks
• Each nursing episode triggers a 10-to-20-fold surge in secretion
• These pulses maintain milk production for subsequent nursing periods

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the nutritional and immunological composition of colostrum with mature breast milk.
back:
• Colostrum: Higher protein/lactose, high antibodies/leukocytes, almost no fat
• Mature milk: Higher fat content and total caloric density (~700 kcal/L)
• Colostrum provides critical early immunity against E. coli

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: List the four metabolic hormones essential for providing the nutrient substrates (glucose, fatty acids, calcium) required for milk formation.
back:
• Growth Hormone (GH)
• Cortisol
• Insulin
• Parathyroid Hormone (PTH)

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The hypothalamus primarily controls prolactin secretion through the continuous release of [___], which acts as the major prolactin inhibitory hormone.
back:
• Dopamine (a catecholamine)
• Transported via hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels
• Inhibits lactotrope synthesis and secretion by up to 10-fold.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A postpartum mother reports that her breasts feel full and heavy, but milk fails to flow when the baby suckles during a period of extreme emotional anxiety. Explain the likely physiological cause.
back:
• Psychogenic inhibition of oxytocin release
• Generalized sympathetic stimulation antagonizes let-down
• Prevents contraction of mammary myoepithelial cells despite adequate milk production.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain the mechanism by which the suckling stimulus leads to increased milk production in the mammary glands.
back:
• Sensory signals from nipples reach the hypothalamus
• Inhibition of Dopamine (Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone)
• Resultant 10-20 fold surge in Prolactin from anterior pituitary
• Stimulates milk synthesis in alveolar epithelial cells.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A patient with a pituitary stalk transection presents with panhypopituitarism but is found to have persistent spontaneous galactorrhea. Contrast the regulation of Prolactin with other anterior pituitary hormones in this scenario.
back:
• Stalk injury removes hypothalamic stimulatory input for most hormones (e.g., ACTH, TSH)
• Prolactin increases because its primary hypothalamic control is inhibitory (Dopamine)
• Loss of portal transport allows lactotropes to hypersecrete autonomously.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Specify the pharmacological category of drugs used to suppress unwanted lactation by mimicking the primary hypothalamic inhibitory factor.
back:
• Dopamine agonists (e.g., Bromocriptine)
• Bind to lactotrope D2 receptors
• Potently suppress Prolactin secretion to halt milk synthesis.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: In the first few days postpartum, the mammary glands secrete [___], which is distinguished from mature milk by its higher protein/lactose concentration and lack of fat.
back:
• Colostrum
• Contains antibodies and immune cells (IgA, macrophages)
• Produced at 1/100th the rate of subsequent mature milk.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A 4-month postpartum nursing mother has not yet resumed her menstrual cycle. Describe the hormonal application of this 'Lactational Amenorrhea'.
back:
• Suckling-induced Prolactin or nerve signals inhibit GnRH release
• Suppresses pituitary FSH and LH secretion
• Prevents ovarian follicular growth and ovulation.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the mechanical processes of milk 'production' versus milk 'ejection' as they relate to specific mammary cell types.
back:
• Production: Prolactin-driven synthesis within alveolar epithelial cells
• Ejection: Oxytocin-driven contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding alveoli
• Ejection (let-down) forces milk into the lactiferous ducts.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the effects of breast-feeding on the maternal Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Ovarian (HPO) axis versus the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Mammary axis.
back:
• HPO Axis: Negative feedback; inhibition of GnRH leads to suppressed fertility
• Mammary Axis: Positive neuroendocrine reflex; suckling drives Prolactin/Oxytocin for milk delivery.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Identify the primary source of the 2 to 3 grams of calcium phosphate lost daily by the mother during peak lactation.
back:
• Maternal bone reservoir
• Parathyroid glands enlarge to increase PTH secretion
• Stimulates bone decalcification to maintain milk mineral levels.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
coreConcept: Milk Ejection Reflex and Myoepithelial Contraction
front: In the mechanism of milk ejection, the posterior pituitary hormone [___] binds to receptors on [___] cells to cause contraction and expression of milk into the ducts.
back:
• Oxytocin.
• Myoepithelial cells (which surround the mammary alveoli).
• This process is known as the milk let-down reflex, occurring within 30-60 seconds of suckling.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A 3-month postpartum female who is exclusively breastfeeding remains amenorrheic. Explain the hormonal basis for this suppression of the ovarian cycle.
back:
• Suckling-induced signals to the hypothalamus inhibit GnRH secretion.
• This leads to suppressed FSH and LH levels from the anterior pituitary.
• High prolactin levels may also directly interfere with ovarian responses to gonadotropins.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain the neuroendocrine mechanism by which suckling maintains continuous milk production over several months.
back:
• Nipple stimulation sends sensory signals to the hypothalamus.
• This causes a 10- to 20-fold surge in Prolactin from the anterior pituitary.
• Prolactin acts on mammary alveolar cells to stimulate milk synthesis for the next feeding.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the primary physiological roles of Prolactin and Oxytocin in the lactating breast.
back:
• Prolactin: Stimulates milk secretion and production within the alveolar epithelial cells.
• Oxytocin: Causes milk ejection (let-down) by contracting myoepithelial cells.
• Prolactin is an anterior pituitary hormone; Oxytocin is from the posterior pituitary.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain why copious milk secretion does not occur during pregnancy despite the 10- to 20-fold increase in prolactin levels.
back:
• High concentrations of Estrogen and Progesterone from the placenta inhibit the actual secretion of milk.
• They render the breast tissue unresponsive to the lactogenic effect of prolactin until after parturition.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The primary hypothalamic controller of prolactin is [___], which acts to [___] its secretion into the portal blood.
back:
• Dopamine (also known as Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone/PIH).
• Inhibit/Decrease.
• Damage to the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system usually results in increased prolactin levels due to loss of this tonic inhibition.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A lactating mother experiences milk leaking from her breasts merely by hearing her infant cry in the next room. Identify the physiological trigger and the hormone responsible.
back:
• Psychic/Emotional stimulus to the hypothalamus.
• Oxytocin.
• Emotional signals can override the physical suckling requirement to trigger the milk let-down reflex.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Describe the specific hormonal synergy required for the development of the mammary lobule-alveolar system during pregnancy.
back:
• Progesterone is the primary driver for alveolar budding.
• It acts synergistically with Estrogen, Growth Hormone, Prolactin, Adrenal Glucocorticoids, and Insulin.
• This converts the breast into a fully developed secretory organ.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the composition of colostrum with mature breast milk.
back:
• Colostrum: Higher concentration of proteins and antibodies; contains almost no fat.
• Mature Milk: Higher fat content and lactose.
• Colostrum is secreted during the first few days post-delivery before mature milk begins.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Identify the primary protective immunological agents found in human breast milk that prevent neonatal enteric infections.
back:
• Secretory IgA antibodies.
• Macrophages and Neutrophils.
• These specifically target and destroy bacteria like Escherichia coli, which can cause lethal diarrhea in newborns.

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: During the latter half of pregnancy, the mother's [___] increases by approximately 15% as a result of increased thyroxine and sex hormone secretion.
back:
* Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR)
* Leads to sensations of being overheated
* Necessitates higher energy expenditure for physical activity

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A pregnant patient at 32 weeks gestation presents with high blood pressure and excessive weight gain. Pathological examination reveals a failure of trophoblasts to adequately remodel [___].
back:
* Maternal spiral arteries
* Results in high-resistance placental vessels
* Triggers placental ischemia and maternal endothelial dysfunction

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Explain the hormonal mechanism and physiological importance of the 30% increase in maternal blood volume observed at term.
back:
* Aldosterone and estrogens stimulate renal salt and water retention
* Bone marrow increases red blood cell production
* Buffers against blood loss during parturition

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the renal hemodynamic changes (GFR and renal blood flow) in a healthy pregnant woman with those found in a patient suffering from preeclampsia.
back:
* Normal: Renal blood flow and GFR increase by ~50% due to vasodilation
* Preeclampsia: Renal blood flow and GFR decrease due to arterial spasm and glomerular damage

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Identify the two specific maternal nutritional stores that are most heavily depleted to meet fetal demands for hematopoiesis and skeletal ossification.
back:
* Iron: Fetal hemoglobin synthesis consumes maternal storage depots
* Calcium: Fetal bone ossification draws from maternal extracellular fluid/bones
* Vitamin D/K supplementation is often essential

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: In the diagnostic assessment of toxemia of pregnancy, the rapid rise in blood pressure is typically associated with the presence of [___] and edema.
back:
* Proteinuria
* Result of thickened glomerular tufts and protein deposits
* Indicates systemic vascular endothelial impairment

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: A woman in her third trimester with untreated preeclampsia suddenly develops generalized clonic seizures followed by a coma. Identify the condition and its immediate management.
back:
* Eclampsia
* Requires immediate rapidly acting vasodilators
* Followed by termination of pregnancy (e.g., Cesarean section)

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Describe the specific physiological mechanism involving progesterone that alters the mother’s respiratory status during pregnancy.
back:
* Increases the sensitivity of the respiratory center to carbon dioxide
* Results in a 50% increase in minute ventilation
* Lowers arterial PCO2 slightly below non-pregnant levels

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Contrast the maternal parathyroid gland activity during pregnancy with its activity during the lactation period.
back:
* Pregnancy: Glands enlarge to maintain calcium during fetal bone ossification
* Lactation: Glands enlarge significantly more to provide calcium for milk production
* Prolonged lactation risks maternal bone decalcification

category: Response of the mother’s body to pregnancy
front: Outline the primary anatomical and physiological changes in the maternal urinary system during a normal pregnancy.
back:
* GFR and renal blood flow increase by ~50%
* Renal tubular reabsorption of salt and water increases by ~50%
* Dilation of ureters increases the risk of urinary stasis

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The milk ejection (let-down) reflex is mediated by the contraction of [___] cells, which form a contractile latticework surrounding the mammary alveoli.
back:
• Myoepithelial cells
• Stimulated by oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
• Forces milk from the alveoli into the lactiferous ducts.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: A 24-year-old nursing mother reports that milk flow begins simply by hearing her infant cry in the next room. This anticipatory milk ejection is primarily mediated by the hormone [___].
back:
• Oxytocin
• Synthesized in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei
• Triggered by psychic, auditory, or tactile stimuli via the hypothalamus.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Explain the physiological mechanism that prevents copious milk secretion during the third trimester of pregnancy despite 10- to 20-fold increases in maternal prolactin.
back:
• High levels of placental estrogen and progesterone
• These steroids directly inhibit the lactogenic effects of prolactin
• Postpartum steroid withdrawal allows milk production to commence.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Contrast the structural roles of estrogen and progesterone in the development of the mammary glands during gestation.
back:
• Estrogen: Stimulates ductal system branching and fat deposition
• Progesterone: Stimulates lobule-alveolar development and alveolar secretory differentiation
• Both are required for complete functional maturity.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: Identify the primary hypothalamic factor that must be suppressed to permit the surge of prolactin necessary for sustained milk production.
back:
• Dopamine (Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone)
• Secreted by arcuate nuclei into the portal system
• Suckling inhibits dopamine release to stimulate the anterior pituitary.

category: Explain the physiology of lactation
front: The suppression of the female ovarian cycle during breastfeeding (lactational amenorrhea) is caused by the inhibition of [___] release by the hypothalamus.
back:
• Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)
• Results in decreased LH and FSH secretion
• Mediated by suckling-induced signals or high prolactin levels.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
coreConcept: Biochemical Structure and Source of Prolactin
front: Prolactin is a single-chain peptide hormone containing [___] amino acids, primarily secreted by the lactotrope cells of the anterior pituitary gland.
back:
• 198 amino acids
• Secreted by lactotropes (mammotropes)
• Constitutes 3% to 5% of anterior pituitary cells
• Promotes mammary development and milk production.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
coreConcept: Tonic Inhibition of Prolactin by Dopamine
front: A 30-year-old female with a pituitary stalk injury presents with high serum prolactin levels despite low levels of other anterior pituitary hormones. Identify the primary neurotransmitter responsible for this finding.
back:
• Dopamine
• Also known as Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone (PIH)
• Unlike other pituitary hormones, prolactin is under tonic hypothalamic inhibition
• Stalk damage prevents dopamine from reaching lactotropes.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Explain the neural reflex mechanism by which nursing a baby leads to a massive 10- to 20-fold surge in prolactin secretion.
back:
• Suckling stimulates nipple mechanoreceptors
• Signals travel to the hypothalamus via somatic nerves
• Hypothalamus inhibits dopamine (PIH) secretion
• Loss of inhibition triggers a rapid surge in prolactin release.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the effects of estrogen and progesterone on the breasts during pregnancy versus their effect on the action of prolactin.
back:
• Breast Development: Estrogen/Progesterone promote physical growth of ducts and lobule-alveolar systems
• Milk Secretion: High levels of these steroids during pregnancy specifically inhibit the lactogenic effect of prolactin.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Identify the four metabolic hormones required as a background 'synergy' for prolactin to successfully facilitate milk formation.
back:
• Growth Hormone
• Cortisol
• Parathyroid Hormone
• Insulin
• These provide necessary amino acids, fatty acids, glucose, and calcium for milk synthesis.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: In nursing mothers, high prolactin levels often suppress the ovarian cycle by inhibiting the hypothalamic release of [___].
back:
• GnRH (Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone)
• Suppresses the surge of LH and FSH
• Results in amenorrhea and temporary infertility (lactational amenorrhea)
• Effect diminishes as nursing frequency decreases.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A postpartum woman fails to produce milk immediately after delivery but begins producing copious amounts 3 days later. Describe the hormonal trigger for this delayed onset.
back:
• Delivery of the placenta causes a sudden drop in Estrogen and Progesterone
• This removes the steroid-mediated inhibition of prolactin
• Prolactin can then activate the alveolar cells for milk secretion.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Directly explain why a patient with severe primary hypothyroidism may also present with galactorrhea (abnormal milk production).
back:
• Primary hypothyroidism causes elevated Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (TRH)
• TRH from the hypothalamus has a secondary stimulatory effect on lactotropes
• Excess TRH leads to hyperprolactinemia and inappropriate milk production.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the composition of the fluid secreted during the first few days postpartum (colostrum) with mature breast milk under prolactin's influence.
back:
• Colostrum: Higher protein and lactose; contains almost no fat
• Mature Milk: Higher fat content and total volume
• Colostrum volume is 1/100th of mature milk production.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Identify the specific site in the hypothalamus where the prolactin-inhibiting factor (dopamine) is primarily produced.
back:
• Arcuate nuclei
• Dopamine is released into the median eminence
• Transported via the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels to the anterior pituitary.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: The primary anterior pituitary hormone responsible for promoting mammary gland development and the synthesis of milk is [___].
back:
• Prolactin (PRL).
• It stimulates alveolar growth and induces milk protein production.
• Full milk secretion only occurs postpartum once estrogen/progesterone inhibition is removed.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A 28-year-old female presents with milky nipple discharge and secondary amenorrhea. An MRI reveals a pituitary microadenoma. The hormone produced by this tumor causes amenorrhea by inhibiting [___].
back:
• Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH).
• High prolactin suppresses the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator.
• This leads to decreased LH and FSH levels, resulting in the cessation of the ovarian cycle.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Explain the unique hypothalamic control of prolactin compared to other anterior pituitary hormones.
back:
• Tonic Inhibition: The hypothalamus primarily inhibits (rather than stimulates) prolactin.
• Mediator: Dopamine (Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone) is the main regulator.
• Stalk Effect: Damage to the pituitary stalk causes prolactin levels to rise.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the specific physiological roles of Prolactin and Oxytocin in the process of lactation.
back:
• Prolactin: Responsible for milk production and secretion into the mammary alveoli (Lactogenesis).
• Oxytocin: Responsible for the milk ejection or 'let-down' reflex via myoepithelial cell contraction (Galactokinesis).

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Identify the primary signaling pathway used by the prolactin receptor to initiate milk protein synthesis.
back:
• JAK-STAT pathway.
• Binding activates Janus Kinase 2 (JAK2).
• This phosphorylates STAT proteins, which translocate to the nucleus to activate gene transcription for milk proteins like casein.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: During pregnancy, the actual secretion of milk is inhibited despite high prolactin levels due to the presence of [___].
back:
• Estrogen and Progesterone.
• These placental steroids promote breast physical development but directly antagonize the lactogenic effects of prolactin on the milk-secreting epithelium.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A patient with hypothalamic damage shows a decrease in TSH, ACTH, and GH, but a significant increase in Prolactin. Describe the mechanism for this paradoxical rise.
back:
• Loss of Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone (Dopamine).
• Other hormones lose their 'releasing factors,' but prolactin is released from chronic dopaminergic inhibition.
• This is often called the 'Stalk Effect.'

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Describe the physiological trigger that causes the 10- to 20-fold transient surge in prolactin secretion in a nursing mother.
back:
• Suckling stimulus.
• Sensory impulses from the nipple travel to the hypothalamus.
• This inhibits dopamine release and possibly stimulates prolactin-releasing factors, maintaining milk production for subsequent feedings.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the levels of Prolactin in a nursing mother versus a non-nursing mother during the postpartum weeks.
back:
• Nursing Mother: Basal levels return to normal, but suckling causes sharp, intermittent spikes for many months.
• Non-nursing Mother: Prolactin levels return to the non-pregnant basal state within 1–2 weeks.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Which hypothalamic tripeptide serves as a potent stimulator of both TSH and Prolactin release?
back:
• Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH).
• While dopamine is the primary inhibitor, TRH can stimulate lactotropes.
• This explains why primary hypothyroidism can sometimes present with galactorrhea.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: The primary hypothalamic neurotransmitter that tonically inhibits the secretion of prolactin by the anterior pituitary is [___].
back:
• Dopamine (also known as Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone).
• It is secreted by the arcuate nuclei and transported via hypothalamic-hypophysial portal vessels.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A 28-year-old nursing mother has not resumed her ovarian cycle 6 months after delivery. The physiological suppression of her GnRH secretion in this state is primarily due to [___].
back:
• High levels of prolactin or suckling-induced nervous signals.
• This inhibits Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH), subsequently suppressing LH and FSH release.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Explain the role of the suckling stimulus in the acute regulation of prolactin secretion.
back:
• Suckling triggers sensory signals from the nipple to the hypothalamus.
• This causes a sharp inhibition of dopamine release.
• Results in a rapid surge of prolactin to promote milk production for future nursing.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the primary biological actions of prolactin and oxytocin regarding lactation.
back:
• Prolactin: Stimulates milk production and secretion into the mammary alveoli.
• Oxytocin: Causes milk ejection (let-down) by contracting myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Identify the four metabolic 'background' hormones required for prolactin to effectively induce milk formation.
back:
• Growth Hormone.
• Cortisol.
• Parathyroid Hormone (PTH).
• Insulin.
• These provide the necessary amino acids, fatty acids, glucose, and calcium.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: In the anterior pituitary, prolactin is synthesized and secreted by specific acidophilic cells called [___].
back:
• Lactotropes (or mammotropes).
• These cells constitute a small portion of the gland but increase during pregnancy.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A patient suffers a traumatic injury to the hypothalamic-hypophysial stalk. While other anterior pituitary hormones decrease, prolactin levels rise. Explain the pathophysiology.
back:
• Disconnection hyperprolactinemia.
• Loss of the inhibitory influence of hypothalamic dopamine (PIH) allows lactotropes to secrete prolactin autonomously.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Explain why copious milk secretion does not occur during pregnancy despite high prolactin levels.
back:
• Estrogen and progesterone (from the placenta) exert a direct suppressive effect.
• They inhibit the actual secretion of milk from the alveoli until after delivery.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the hypothalamic control of prolactin with the control of TSH and ACTH.
back:
• TSH/ACTH: Primarily regulated by hypothalamic releasing hormones (TRH/CRH).
• Prolactin: Primarily regulated by a hypothalamic inhibitory factor (Dopamine).

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: List the non-reproductive physiological factors known to stimulate prolactin secretion.
back:
• Sleep (surges occur during sleep).
• Stress and trauma.
• Exercise.
• Thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) can also act as a minor stimulator.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: The primary hypothalamic transmitter responsible for the tonic inhibition of prolactin secretion from the lactotropes is [___].
back:
• Dopamine
• Also known as Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone (PIH)
• Secreted by the arcuate nuclei of the hypothalamus into the portal system.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A postpartum woman exclusively breastfeeding her infant remains amenorrheic for several months. Describe the pathophysiology underlying this temporary infertility.
back:
• Prolactin (or nursing-induced nervous signals) inhibits the secretion of Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH).
• This suppresses LH and FSH release, preventing the restart of the ovarian cycle.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Explain why copious milk production does not occur during pregnancy despite prolactin levels rising 10-20 times above normal.
back:
• Placental estrogen and progesterone prepare the breasts but specifically inhibit the actual secretion of milk.
• Birth triggers the sudden loss of these steroids, allowing prolactin's lactogenic effects to manifest.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the roles of Prolactin and Oxytocin in the functional physiology of lactation.
back:
• Prolactin: Stimulates milk synthesis and production within the mammary alveoli.
• Oxytocin: Causes milk ejection (let-down) by contracting myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Identify the non-pituitary hypothalamic hormone that stimulates prolactin secretion and may cause galactorrhea in primary hypothyroid states.
back:
• Thyrotropin-Releasing Hormone (TRH)
• TRH stimulates both TSH and prolactin; in hypothyroidism, elevated TRH levels can cause pathological hyperprolactinemia.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Prolactin is a protein hormone synthesized in the anterior pituitary by a single chain containing [___] amino acids.
back:
• 198 amino acids
• Synthesized by Acidophilic cells known as Lactotropes (or mammotropes).

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A nursing mother experiences a sudden surge in prolactin levels lasting about 60 minutes. Identify the specific stimulus and neural pathway responsible for this event.
back:
• Stimulus: Suckling on the nipple.
• Pathway: Sensory nerves transmit signals from the nipple to the hypothalamus, reducing dopamine inhibition to allow a massive prolactin surge.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Describe how Prolactin regulation differs fundamentally from the regulation of Growth Hormone or ACTH.
back:
• GH and ACTH: Primarily controlled by hypothalamic releasing factors (stimulatory).
• Prolactin: Primarily controlled by hypothalamic inhibitory factors (tonic dopamine inhibition).

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the requirement of metabolic hormones needed to support prolactin-mediated milk formation.
back:
• Prolactin is the specific driver, but successful lactation requires metabolic support from:
• Insulin, Cortisol, Growth Hormone, and Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) to provide necessary nutrients.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: What is colostrum, and how does its composition differ from mature breast milk?
back:
• Secreted in the first days postpartum.
• Contains same protein and lactose concentrations as mature milk.
• Lacks fat and is produced at 1/100 the volume of mature milk.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: The primary hypothalamic factor that exerts tonic inhibitory control over the secretion of prolactin by anterior pituitary lactotropes is [___].
back:
● Dopamine (Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone).
● Secreted by neurons in the arcuate nuclei.
● Transported via the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: A 29-year-old female presents with galactorrhea and secondary amenorrhea. Labs confirm hyperprolactinemia. The pathophysiology of her cessation of menses is the prolactin-mediated suppression of [___].
back:
● Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH).
● Prolactin inhibits GnRH pulses from the hypothalamus.
● Leads to decreased FSH and LH secretion, causing anovulation.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Explain why copious milk production is absent during pregnancy despite prolactin levels rising up to 20 times the normal non-pregnant value.
back:
● Steroid Inhibition: High levels of placental Estrogen and Progesterone.
● These steroids inhibit the actual secretory action of prolactin on mammary alveoli.
● Effect is removed only after delivery of the placenta.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Contrast the specific physiological actions of Prolactin and Oxytocin on the mammary glands during the postpartum period.
back:
● Prolactin: Stimulates milk production and secretion into the mammary alveoli.
● Oxytocin: Causes contraction of myoepithelial cells for milk ejection ("let-down").

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: Describe the temporal secretory pattern of prolactin in a nursing mother several weeks after parturition.
back:
● Basal levels return to non-pregnant values.
● Intermittent Surges: 10- to 20-fold increases occur for approximately 1 hour during each nursing episode.

category: Discuss the actions of prolactin
front: The maintenance of milk production during lactation requires the intermittent surge of prolactin, which is triggered by nervous signals originating from the [___].
back:
● Nipples (Suckling Stimulus).
● Signals travel to the hypothalamus to inhibit dopamine and stimulate prolactin release.
● Absence of suckling causes milk loss within approximately one week.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Although prolactin levels are high during pregnancy, actual milk secretion is inhibited by the direct suppressive effects of [___] and [___] from the placenta.
back:
* Estrogen and Progesterone.
* These steroids inhibit the lactogenic effect of Prolactin.
* Copious milk production only begins after the sudden postpartum drop of these hormones.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: A 28-year-old female in her 36th week of gestation has well-developed mammary glands but produces only a few milliliters of colostrum. Explain the hormonal basis for the absence of copious milk production.
back:
* High placental Estrogen and Progesterone levels.
* They stimulate physical development of breast tissue but antagonize Prolactin's secretory action.
* This prevents large-scale milk production until after delivery.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Describe how suckling by a neonate maintains the suppression of the ovarian cycle in a nursing mother.
back:
* Suckling sends sensory signals to the hypothalamus.
* These signals inhibit the pulsatile release of GnRH.
* Low GnRH results in suppressed FSH and LH, preventing follicular growth and ovulation.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Contrast the physiological stimulus required for the "secretion" of milk versus the "ejection" (let-down) of milk in a postpartum female.
back:
* Secretion: Primarily driven by Prolactin from the anterior pituitary.
* Ejection: Driven by Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary causing myoepithelial contraction.
* Both are triggered by suckling-induced neuroendocrine reflexes.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Identify the neurotransmitter released by the arcuate nuclei that acts as the primary Prolactin-Inhibiting Hormone (PIH).
back:
* Dopamine.
* It is secreted into the hypothalamic-hypophysial portal system.
* It provides tonic inhibition of prolactin release from the anterior pituitary lactotropes.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: The physiological term for the suppression of the female monthly sexual cycle during the nursing period is [___].
back:
* Lactational Amenorrhea.
* Caused by suckling-induced suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis.
* This serves as a natural, though not absolute, birth-spacing mechanism.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: A nursing mother notices that her milk flows not only during suckling but also when she hears her baby cry. Explain the underlying neuroendocrine reflex.
back:
* Psychic signals trigger the posterior pituitary.
* This causes a surge of Oxytocin release.
* Oxytocin induces contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, resulting in milk let-down.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Explain the physiological shift that occurs 1 to 7 days after delivery that allows the breasts to begin secreting copious milk.
back:
* Loss of placental Estrogen and Progesterone removes the inhibitory block on Prolactin.
* Prolactin stimulates alveolar cells to produce milk nutrients (casein, lactose, fat).
* Adequate background levels of Growth Hormone and Cortisol are required.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
coreConcept: Dual Role of Progesterone in Breast Physiology
front: Contrast the effects of Progesterone on breast development during pregnancy versus its effect on lactation itself.
back:
* Development: Progesterone promotes lobule-alveolar growth and secretory differentiation.
* Lactation: It directly inhibits actual milk secretion into the alveoli by antagonizing Prolactin’s intracellular effects.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Identify the specific mammary cell type that contracts to force milk from the alveoli into the ducts during the milk let-down reflex.
back:
* Myoepithelial cells.
* These cells form a contractile latticework around the alveoli.
* They possess receptors for Oxytocin and respond within seconds to suckling.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: During pregnancy, the high concentrations of [___] and [___] secreted by the placenta promote structural development of the breasts but directly inhibit the lactogenic effect of prolactin, thereby suppressing milk secretion.
back:
• Estrogen
• Progesterone
• These steroids block the final action of prolactin on mammary alveoli until delivery.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: A 30-year-old G1P0 at 39 weeks gestation reports breast enlargement and colostrum leaks but no active milk production. Identify the physiological event immediately following delivery that will trigger copious milk secretion.
back:
• Sudden withdrawal of placental estrogen and progesterone
• This allows the high levels of prolactin to exert their full lactogenic effect on the breast tissue.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Explain the role of the suckling-induced neuroendocrine reflex in maintaining lactational amenorrhea in nursing mothers.
back:
• Suckling sends sensory signals to the hypothalamus
• This inhibits Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH) secretion
• Decreased GnRH suppresses pituitary FSH and LH, preventing follicle maturation and ovulation.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Contrast the hormonal requirements for the structural growth of breast ductules versus the development of the lobule-alveolar system during pregnancy.
back:
• Ductules: Primarily stimulated by Estrogen (plus GH, prolactin, and insulin).
• Lobule-Alveolar System: Requires Progesterone acting synergistically with estrogen and other metabolic hormones.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: Name the primary hypothalamic neurotransmitter that acts as the 'Prolactin Inhibitory Hormone' (PIH).
back:
• Dopamine
• Secreted by the arcuate nuclei of the hypothalamus into the portal system to tonically inhibit prolactin.

category: Justify the suppression of ejection of milk during pregnancy Discuss the physiological basis of suppression of the female ovarian cycles in nursing mothers for many months after delivery
front: The suppression of the female ovarian cycle in nursing mothers is fundamentally due to the inhibition of [___] release from the hypothalamus, which prevents the preovulatory surge of LH.
back:
• Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone (GnRH)
• This effect is strongest in mothers who breastfeed exclusively and frequently.
